Fundamental Rights

1. Purpose, scope and six groups

  • Part III, 12–35; US Bill of Rights influence; “Magna Carta of India”. Protect dignity, liberty, equality, minorities and political democracy; restrain arbitrary government and support rule of law. Magna Carta dates to 1215; avoid calling it history's first-ever rights document.
  • Six groups: Equality 14–18; Freedom 19–22/21A; Against exploitation 23–24; Religion 25–28; Cultural/educational 29–30; Remedies 32.
  • Originally seven: property under 19(1)(f)/31; 44th Amendment 1978 removed it from Fundamental Rights; 300A, Part XII now protects property as a constitutional legal right.
  • Rights are justiciable, contain positive/negative obligations and have provision-specific limits. Some protect citizens, others all persons; legal persons can claim compatible rights, but a company is not itself a citizen for Article 19.
  • 15, 16, 19, 29 expressly protect citizens; 14, 20, 21, 23–28 generally protect persons. 21A: children 6–14. Article 30 is not simply worded citizen-only; enemy-alien exclusions apply specifically, not to all rights indiscriminately.
  • Rights bind the State; some expressly reach private conduct (15(2), 17, 23, 24). Kaushal Kishor (2023) also rejects a blanket claim that Articles 19/21 can never operate against private actors. Supreme Court
  • Parliament can amend rights only through constitutional procedure and within basic structure; ordinary law can regulate within permitted limits, not simply repeal constitutional guarantees.

2. State and law: Articles 12–13

  • 12—State includes: Union Government/Parliament; State governments/legislatures; local authorities; other authorities. Instrumentality/agency analysis depends on control, functions and other judicial tests; neither every private body nor every government-linked organisation is automatically State.
  • 13: inconsistent laws void to extent of inconsistency. Includes legislation, ordinances, orders, rules, regulations, notifications, bye-laws and customs/usages with force of law.
  • Judicial review: SC 32, HC 226. Article 13(4) excludes Article 368 amendments from its ordinary-law rule, but amendments remain reviewable for basic-structure damage.

3. Equality: Article 14 and rule of law

  • Equality before law: British influence, no special privilege/above-law status. Equal protection: American influence, like treatment in like circumstances. Negative restraint and positive equal treatment complement each other.
  • Reasonable classification requires intelligible differentia + rational nexus to the law's objective. Unequals may require different treatment; Article 14 still governs that distinction. Arbitrary class legislation is forbidden.
  • Dicey: absence of arbitrary power; equality before ordinary law; individual rights as foundation of Constitution. India's written Constitution supplies rights, so the third aspect is not adopted in the same form. Rule of law is basic structure.
  • 361: President/Governor personal constitutional immunities; no criminal proceedings/arrest during term; specified personal civil proceedings require two months' notice. Their actions/government decisions are not thereby beyond judicial review.
  • 361A: substantially true legislative-proceeding reports protected, with exceptions including malice and secret sittings. 105/194: legislative speech/vote privileges; not blanket criminal immunity.
  • Foreign sovereign/diplomatic/UN immunities depend on applicable law/treaties; Article 31C supplies limited protection for qualifying 39(b)/(c) laws.

4. Article 15: prohibited discrimination and protective measures

  • 15(1): State cannot discriminate against citizens only on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. Other classifications remain subject to equality scrutiny; “only” does not authorise arbitrary discrimination.
  • 15(2): public access to shops, restaurants, hotels, entertainment and specified public-use wells/tanks/roads/resorts; reaches private as well as State conduct.
  • 15(3): special provisions for women/children. 15(4): socially/educationally backward classes, SCs/STs—1st Amendment 1951.
  • 15(5): admissions measures including private aided/unaided institutions, excluding Article 30 minority institutions—93rd Amendment 2005. Central educational reservation legislation 2006, OBC 27%, upheld with creamy-layer exclusion 2008.
  • 15(6): EWS measures/admission reservation up to 10%, additional to existing reservations; minority-institution exception; 103rd Amendment 2019. Janhit Abhiyan 2022: amendment upheld 3:2. SC account of majority ruling

5. OBC creamy layer and EWS criteria

  • OBC creamy layer is not merely a universal income test. Parental status/service rank, professional/business/land categories and prescribed income/wealth tests matter; Group A/B, equivalent posts and Colonel/equivalent cases have detailed conditions.
  • Income-ceiling history: ₹1 lakh 1993; ₹2.5 lakh 2004; ₹4.5 lakh 2008; ₹6 lakh 2013; ₹8 lakh 2017. Apply rules on income sources and parental status, not an undifferentiated salary total. Official ceiling notification
  • Central EWS scheme 2019: persons outside SC/ST/OBC reservation coverage; family gross annual income below ₹8 lakh, including specified income sources in preceding financial year.
  • Excluded if family owns 5+ acres agricultural land; 1,000+ sq ft residential flat; 100+ sq yd plot in notified municipality; 200+ sq yd plot elsewhere, regardless of income. Aggregate property across locations.
  • Family: applicant, parents, siblings under 18, spouse and children under 18. Scheme eligibility is administrative, distinct from constitutional text; State criteria can differ under applicable law.

6. Article 16 and reservation chronology

  • 16(1)–(2): equal public-employment opportunity; prohibited grounds additionally include descent/residence. 16(3): Parliament can prescribe specified residence requirements; 371D arrangements for AP/Telangana are distinct.
  • 16(4): backward classes inadequately represented. 16(4A): SC/ST promotion reservation, 77th 1995; consequential seniority, 85th 2001, retrospective June 1995. Enabling provisions remain subject to judicial conditions; not automatic compulsory reservation in every post.
  • 16(4B): separate treatment of backlog reserved vacancies—81st 2000. 16(5): specified religious/denominational office qualifications. 16(6): EWS up to 10%, 103rd 2019.
  • Kalelkar: first Backward Classes Commission 1953, report 1955. Mandal: second Commission 1979, report 1980; identified 3,743 castes, estimated 52% population, recommended 27% OBC jobs. These are historical estimates, not current census figures.
  • 1990 V.P. Singh: OBC quota implementation; 1991: poorer-OBC preference and separate 10% economic quota proposed.
  • Indra Sawhney 1992: upheld 27% OBC reservation; exclude creamy layer; ordinary 50% ceiling, extraordinary exceptions; no promotions under 16(4); carry-forward subject to then-law limits; permanent complaints body. Later constitutional provisions changed parts of that framework.
  • Ram Nandan committee 1993: creamy-layer criteria. NCBC statutory 1993 → constitutional 338B under 102nd 2018; 105th 2021 clarified States' own backward-class identification powers.
  • 76th 1994: Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation law in Ninth Schedule—not absolute judicial-review immunity. 82nd 2000: 335 proviso permits specified SC/ST promotion qualifying-mark/evaluation relaxations.
  • Chapter's central EWS scientific/technical exemption requires all three: grade above lowest Group A, recognised scientific/technical classification, and research/organisation/direction of research duties.

7. Articles 17–18: untouchability and titles

  • 17: untouchability abolished; enforceable against private conduct; statutory punishment. Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 → Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955, strengthened/renamed 1976. Concerns historically caste-based disabilities, not every form of social avoidance.
  • PUDR 1982: State must protect against private rights violations. Keep abolition distinct from the wider SC/ST atrocities-law framework.
  • 18: State cannot confer titles except military/academic distinctions; citizens cannot accept foreign-State titles. Foreigners in State office of profit/trust need President's consent for foreign titles; anyone in such office needs consent for specified foreign presents/emoluments/offices.
  • Balaji Raghavan 1995: Bharat Ratna/Padma awards permissible; do not use as name prefixes/suffixes. These are honours, not hereditary nobility.
  • Awards instituted 1954, discontinued 1977, revived 1980; Padma interruptions 1978–79, 1993–97. Chapter's Padma guideline: 120 annually, excluding specified posthumous/foreign/NRI/OCI cases. Its Bharat Ratna “maximum three” should not be memorised as exceptionless: five were conferred in 2024. Official 2024 presentation, Advani presentation

8. Article 19: six freedoms and exact restriction grounds

  • Speech/expression, 19(1)(a)/19(2): sovereignty/integrity; State security; friendly foreign relations; public order; decency/morality; contempt; defamation; incitement to offence—eight grounds.
  • Peaceful unarmed assembly, (b)/(3): sovereignty/integrity, public order. No guaranteed right to violent obstruction or strike; reasonable regulation of time/place applies.
  • Association/unions/cooperatives, (c)/(4): sovereignty/integrity, public order, morality. Includes joining/not joining; recognition, successful bargaining or strike not automatically guaranteed. Cooperatives added by 97th Amendment.
  • Movement/residence, (d)/(e)/(5): general-public interest, Scheduled Tribe interests. Internal movement under 19; foreign travel under 21.
  • Profession/occupation/trade/business, (g)/(6): general-public interest, qualifications and permitted State monopolies; unlawful/harmful activities may be regulated/prohibited.
  • 1st Amendment 1951: speech grounds including friendly relations/public order/incitement and State-monopoly protection; 16th 1963: sovereignty/integrity additions. 19(1)(f) property omitted by 44th.
  • Speech covers press/circulation, commercial speech, silence, access to relevant information/candidate antecedents, broadcasting, reply, gender expression, national-flag expression, lawful protest, film/social-media communication, subject to constitutional limits. Telephone privacy also engages 21; pre-censorship principles differ by medium.
  • Anuradha Bhasin 2020: expression/business through internet protected; restrictions proportionate, indefinite suspension impermissible. This is not an unrestricted right to every internet facility.
  • Old references CrPC 144/IPC 141 are historical: corresponding current provisions are BNSS 163/BNS 189, operational 1 July 2024. An assembly of five is not unlawful merely because of its size; statutory common object matters.
  • Health/area restrictions cited in the chapter are case-specific; no general licence to discriminate against persons with HIV or other vulnerable groups.

9. Article 20: three criminal-law safeguards

  • No retrospective criminal conviction/heavier penalty: law at time of offence controls; beneficial change may operate under law. Not a general bar to retrospective civil/tax legislation.
  • No double jeopardy: prosecuted and punished again for the same offence; departmental action is not automatically prior criminal prosecution. Statutory protections may be wider.
  • No compelled self-incrimination: accused cannot be forced to provide incriminating testimonial evidence. Fingerprints, physical samples or specimen signatures are not automatically testimonial confession; privacy/procedural safeguards still apply.
  • Applies to persons including foreigners; 20 and 21 enforcement cannot be suspended under 359.

10. Article 21: dignity and fair procedure

  • Life/personal liberty can be deprived only by procedure established by law. A.K. Gopalan 1950: narrow approach; Maneka Gandhi 1978: procedure must be just, fair, reasonable, consistent with 14/19/21.
  • Life includes dignity, not mere survival. Rights recognised through cases have context and lawful limits; not every desirable benefit is an unconditional individual entitlement.
  • Dignity/welfare: livelihood, shelter, health/emergency care, educational opportunity, family-pension/insurance interests, social/economic justice, fair opportunity, women's dignity, choice of partner, decent burial/cremation.
  • Fair justice/detention: legal aid, speedy/fair trial, appeal safeguards, humane prisoner necessities; protection against bonded labour, custody abuse, unjustified handcuffs/bar fetters/solitary confinement, inhuman treatment, delayed execution/public hanging.
  • Personal autonomy/information: privacy, reputation, foreign travel, information, protection against unjust displacement from a State. Marriage choice ≠ automatic judicial recognition of every marital status.
  • Environment/living conditions: clean air/water, protection from hazardous industry/noise, sleep, sustainable development, access-road issues in context, protection against adverse climate effects (M.K. Ranjitsinh 2024, Articles 14/21).
  • Die with dignity: lawful passive-euthanasia/advance-directive framework, not general right to suicide or active killing.
  • Case map: Satwant Singh 1967—foreign travel; Hoskot 1978—legal aid; Hussainara 1979—speedy trial; Francis Coralie 1981—dignity/prisoner essentials; Sheela Barse 1983—custody safeguards; RLEK 1985—environment; Olga Tellis 1985—livelihood; Parmanand Katara 1989—emergency medical aid; Shantistar 1990—shelter; Puttaswamy 2017—privacy; Common Cause 2018—dying with dignity.

11. Education: 21A, 45 and 51A(k)

  • 86th Amendment 2002: 21A—free compulsory education 6–14; revised 45—early childhood care/education below 6; 51A(k)—parent/guardian educational opportunity, 6–14.
  • RTE Act 2009, operative with relevant amendment provisions 1 April 2010; elementary education with prescribed quality/norms, not unlimited free higher/professional education.
  • Mohini Jain 1992 → Unni Krishnan 1993: education under 21, with economic-capacity qualification beyond childhood; later 21A gives express age-specific guarantee.

12. Article 22: ordinary arrest versus preventive detention

  • Ordinary arrest: informed grounds; consult/defended by lawyer; magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey; further custody needs magistrate authority. Article 22(1)–(2) exceptions: enemy aliens and preventive detention.
  • Punitive detention: criminal process/punishment for offence; preventive: precautionary detention to prevent specified future harmful activity, under law—not punishment after conviction.
  • Preventive safeguards: prompt grounds, earliest representation opportunity; public-interest facts may be withheld under 22(6).
  • Three months without sufficient-cause Advisory Board report is the general constitutional threshold, with 22(7) parliamentary exceptions/maximum-duration machinery. Board members must have prescribed HC judicial qualifications; not necessarily all serving judges.
  • 44th Amendment's two-month change was not commenced; do not substitute it for operative three months.
  • Union exclusive lawmaking: defence, foreign affairs, security of India; concurrent: State security, public order, essential supplies/services.
  • Historical laws: Preventive Detention Act 1950 expired 1969; MISA 1971 repealed 1978; TADA lapsed 1995; POTA 2002 repealed 2004. Relevant preventive statutes include COFEPOSA 1974, NSA 1980, essential-supplies/blackmarketing Act 1980, PITNDPS 1988.
  • UAPA 1967 is principally penal/counterterrorism legislation with special custody/bail rules; do not equate all UAPA custody with constitutional preventive detention. Chapter's “no other democracy” claim is too absolute.

13. Against exploitation: 23–24

  • 23: trafficking, begar (unpaid forced work), bonded/similar forced labour prohibited against State/private actors. Economic compulsion, including legally relevant below-minimum-wage labour, can constitute force (PUDR 1982).
  • Exception: compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination only on religion, race, caste or class. Trafficking/forced exploitation is not identical to all consensual adult sex work.
  • Laws cited: Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976, wage/contract/equal-remuneration frameworks. Four Labour Codes became effective 21 November 2025, consolidating 29 laws; distinguish older Acts from the current framework and its transition/savings provisions. Labour Ministry update
  • 24: children under 14 not employed in factory, mine or hazardous work. Statute goes further: 2016 amendment renamed 1986 law Child and Adolescent Labour Act; general under-14 employment prohibition with narrow family/artist exceptions; adolescents 14–18 barred from hazardous occupations/processes as defined.
  • M.C. Mehta 1996: employer contribution ₹20,000 per child to rehabilitation fund and welfare/education directions. Child Rights Commissions Act 2005: National/State Commissions and Children's Courts; 2006 prohibited-occupation expansion included domestic/hospitality employment.

14. Religion: 25–28

  • 25—all persons: conscience; profess declare belief; practise rituals; propagate explain/disseminate. Does not authorise forced conversion; protect others' conscience and voluntary choice.
  • Limits: public order, morality, health, other Fundamental Rights; State may regulate secular economic/financial/political activities and reform/open public Hindu religious institutions as provided.
  • Kirpan wearing/carrying recognised for Sikhs. Inclusion of Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists as “Hindus” is for the specified institutional-access clause, not a universal religious reclassification.
  • 26—denominations: establish/maintain religious/charitable institutions; manage religious affairs; own/acquire property; administer property according to law. Public-order/morality/health limits apply; wording differs from 25.
  • Denomination: common faith/beliefs, organisation and distinctive name; chapter cites Ramakrishna Mission/Ananda Marga, and rejects Auroville as such in the cited setting.
  • 27: no compulsory tax specifically appropriated to promote/maintain a particular religion/denomination. Regulation/service fees are not automatically such taxes; not a ban on all public spending touching religion.
  • 28: wholly State-funded institution—no religious instruction; State-administered endowment/trust requiring instruction—exception; recognised/aided institution—no compulsory instruction/worship without consent, guardian for minor.

15. Culture and minority education: 29–30

  • 29(1): any section of citizens with distinct language/script/culture may conserve it—not minority-only. 29(2): State-maintained/aided admission cannot be denied only on religion, race, caste, language; note different list from 15.
  • 30: religious/linguistic minorities establish/administer institutions of choice; no minority-status discrimination in aid. Constitution does not define “minority”; relevant judicial framework matters.
  • 30(1A): acquisition amount must not restrict/abrogate protected institutional right, 44th Amendment.
  • Malankara Syrian Catholic College 2006: choose governing body/staff, admit qualified students, reasonable fees, use assets; administration ≠ maladministration.
  • General laws and legitimate academic/staff/welfare/financial-accountability regulation apply. Aided status permits proper-aid conditions but does not erase minority character; unaided institutions retain lawful rational selection freedom.
  • Recognition/aid distinctions do not put unrecognised institutions beyond ordinary law. Minority institutions may teach in their own language within applicable framework.

16. Remedies and five writs

  • 32: enforcement remedy is itself Fundamental Right; Ambedkar—heart and soul. Direct/original SC route for Fundamental Rights; no prior HC appeal inherently necessary. 226: HC remedies for Fundamental Rights and other legal rights; wider subject-matter reach.
  • SC/HC jurisdictions concurrent, not SC exclusive. 32 is guaranteed, 226 discretionary; courts still apply procedural/judicial principles. Parliament may empower other courts under 32(3) without displacing SC powers.
  • Habeas corpus—produce/test custody: against public/private detainer; illegal detention release. Lawful competent-court custody ordinarily not set aside through this route, but jurisdictional/serious illegality cannot be ignored.
  • Mandamus—we command: perform public/legal duty; can reach bodies performing public duties under 226, including some non-State bodies. Not ordinarily private contractual obligation; cannot dictate a particular lawful discretionary choice, though can require discretion be exercised lawfully.
  • Prohibition—forbid: prevent lower judicial/quasi-judicial body's jurisdictional excess while proceedings pending.
  • Certiorari—quash: defective order/jurisdiction/natural-justice error; can reach relevant administrative decisions. Distinguish ongoing prevention from quashing, without treating simplified timing as absolute.
  • Quo warranto—by what authority: legality of holding substantive constitutional/statutory public office; any appropriate public applicant, not only personally injured person. Not private employment; chapter's blanket exclusion of “ministerial office” should not be read as excluding constitutional ministers from all review.

17. Forces, martial law and Parliament's special competence

  • 33: Parliament may restrict/abrogate rights for specified armed/public-order forces, intelligence and connected communications personnel to ensure duty/discipline; State legislature cannot use this power. May include attached non-combatants as legally applicable.
  • Examples: Army/Air Force Acts 1950; Navy Act 1957 (correct chapter's 1950); Police Forces Restrictions Act 1966, BSF legislation. Restrictions must remain within constitutional/statutory authority; not unlimited exemption from review.
  • 34: parliamentary indemnity/validation concerning acts to maintain/restore order where martial law operated. Constitution does not supply a detailed express declaration procedure; Article 34 is not a free-standing unlimited executive military-rule power.
  • Military law: service-discipline law; martial law: extraordinary military administration in affected area; National Emergency 352: detailed constitutional declaration on war/external aggression/armed rebellion, affecting federal and fiscal arrangements as well as rights.
  • National Emergency can apply nationally/partly and ordinary courts continue. Martial law does not automatically suspend habeas corpus; avoid the chapter's unrestricted claims about military punishment of civilians.
  • 35: Parliament's exclusive competence for specified 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 matters and punishments for Part-III-declared offences (17/23); existing laws continue until changed. Not all legislation concerning any right is Parliament-exclusive.

18. Emergency and rights

  • 358: during National Emergency on war/external aggression, Article 19 constraints relaxed within constitutional conditions; not armed rebellion. Relevant law must contain emergency nexus recital and executive action be under such law; territorial qualifications apply.
  • 359: President may suspend court enforcement of specified rights for specified period/territory; 20/21 excluded. It is not automatic abolition of every right during every emergency.

19. Property and protective clauses: 300A, 31A–C

  • 300A: deprivation only by authority of law; HC 226 remedy, not 32 solely for property. Ordinary law may regulate, but legislative deprivation is not immune from constitutional scrutiny; lawful public purpose/procedure/compensation principles matter. Do not memorise “no compensation ever guaranteed”. SC: Kolkata Municipal Corporation, 2024
  • Special protections: minority educational-institution acquisition 30(1A); personal-cultivation land within ceiling 31A—market-value protection. Amendment history: 1st, 4th, 7th, 17th, 25th, 39th, 40th, 42nd, 44th in property/protective-law development.
  • 31A: five specified categories—estates acquisition/rights; management takeover; corporate amalgamation; directors/shareholders' rights; mining leases. Limited shield from 14/19, with President-assent requirement for relevant State laws; not blanket protection against every constitutional ground.
  • 31B + Ninth Schedule, 1st 1951: original 13 laws; chapter 282 surviving entries, serials through 284 with omissions/257A. Waman Rao/Coelho: post-24 April 1973 insertions reviewable for basic-structure damage; a rights violation must be assessed in that framework.
  • 31C, 25th 1971: qualifying laws implementing 39(b)/(c) protected from 14/19 challenges. Court can test whether law genuinely serves those objectives; exclusion of that review invalidated in Kesavananda 1973.
  • 42nd 1976 extension to all DPSPs struck down in Minerva Mills 1980; do not reproduce the invalid extension as operative law.
  • Rights outside Part III include 265—tax by law; 300A—property; 301—trade freedom; 326—adult suffrage. Their enforcement route differs from Article 32, unless another Fundamental Right is also involved.

20. Criticisms, significance and answer structure

  • Criticisms: excessive restrictions (Jaspat Roy Kapoor); incomplete work/social-security guarantees; technical language (Jennings—lawyers' paradise); amendment vulnerability; emergency suspensions; cost of litigation; preventive detention; alleged inconsistent philosophy.
  • Balance: basic structure, judicial review, legal aid/PIL and expanded 21/21A constrain these weaknesses. Constitutional social/economic interests are not wholly absent; some appear in DPSPs/statutes and evolving rights interpretation.
  • Significance: democracy, material/moral development, rule of law, liberty, minority/weaker-section protection, secularism, accountable government, social justice, dignity and political participation.
  • Mains: identify right and beneficiary → explain permissible limits → cite relevant case → distinguish enforceability/exception → evaluate liberty with constitutional public interest.

chapters.markdown:
# Directive Principles of State Policy

## 1. Nature, origin and constitutional role

- **Part IV, 36–51:** 36 defines State as in Part III; **37** states nature/duty; substantive directives mainly **38–51**. **Irish Constitution 1937** influence, with Spanish antecedents.
- **Ambedkar—novel features/instructions to legislature and executive**; parallels the **1935 Act's Instrument of Instructions**. **Granville Austin: Rights + DPSPs = conscience of the Constitution**.
- Aim: welfare State, social/economic democracy and Preamble's justice/liberty/equality/fraternity; go beyond a State confined to policing and defence.
- **Not independently enforceable in court**, but **fundamental in governance**; State has a constitutional duty to apply them in lawmaking. Political accountability/public opinion supply the principal sanction.
- Courts use them to interpret rights and assess statutory purpose/reasonableness; implementing a DPSP does **not automatically cure every constitutional violation**.
- **B.N. Rau:** justiciable/non-justiciable distinction. Reasons for non-justiciability: resource limits, diverse/backward conditions and flexibility over timing/priorities for the new State.

![Non-justiciability does not make directives optional.](Revision%20Diagrams/nature.svg)

*Non-justiciability does not make directives optional.*

## 2. Socialistic principles: justice and welfare

- **38:** just social order; reduce income/status/facility/opportunity inequalities among individuals and groups.
- **39(a):** adequate livelihood for men/women equally; **(b):** material resources distributed for common good; **(c):** avoid wealth/production concentration to common detriment.
- **39(d):** equal pay for equal work; **(e):** protect worker health/strength and children from abuse/economic compulsion; **(f):** healthy development, dignity and childhood/youth protection from exploitation/abandonment.
- **39A:** equal justice/free legal aid. **41:** work, education and public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness/disability and undeserved want, **within economic capacity/development**.
- **42:** humane working conditions and maternity relief. **43:** living wage, decent life, leisure/social/cultural opportunity. **43A:** worker participation in management. **47:** nutrition, living standards and public health.
- Wage distinction: **minimum—basic statutory protection; fair—between minimum and living in textbook formulation; living—decent life including wider education/health/social needs**. Actual wage law, not this mnemonic alone, determines entitlement.

## 3. Gandhian principles

- **40:** village Panchayats with self-government powers. **43:** rural cottage industries on individual/cooperative basis.
- **43B:** voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control and professional cooperative management.
- **46:** weaker sections, particularly SCs/STs—education/economic interests and protection from injustice/exploitation.
- **47:** prohibit harmful intoxicating drinks/drugs **except medicinal purposes**. **48:** preserve/improve breeds; prohibit slaughter of cows/calves and other milch/draught cattle.
- Categories are **textbook classifications, not constitutional headings**; one Article can serve more than one category.

## 4. Liberal-intellectual principles

- **44:** Uniform Civil Code for citizens. **45:** early childhood care/education **below six**.
- **48:** scientific agriculture/animal husbandry. **48A:** environment, forests and wildlife.
- **49:** protect monuments/places/objects of artistic/historic interest **declared of national importance**.
- **50:** judiciary–executive separation in State public services. **51:** international peace/security, just honourable relations, respect for international law/treaties, arbitration.

![Use categories to remember purposes, not as constitutional compartments.](Revision%20Diagrams/classification.svg)

*Use categories to remember purposes, not as constitutional compartments.*

## 5. Amendment additions: high-yield sequence

- **42nd, 1976—four changes:** healthy child development **39(f)**; free legal aid **39A**; worker management participation **43A**; environment **48A**.
- **44th, 1978:** minimise specified inequalities **38(2)**.
- **86th, 2002:** **45** changed from original under-14 education goal to **below-six care/education**; **21A** makes 6–14 education a right; **51A(k)** gives parental/guardian duty. Relevant provisions operational **2010**.
- **97th, 2011:** **43B cooperatives**, effective **2012**. Judicial invalidation of Part IXB for State-only cooperatives does **not remove 43B**.

![Recall additions separately from their commencement and judicial limits.](Revision%20Diagrams/amendments.svg)

*Recall additions separately from their commencement and judicial limits.*

## 6. Rights versus DPSPs: compare without overstatement

- **Rights:** enforceable constitutional guarantees, legal remedies, political democracy plus dignity/social aspects; **DPSPs:** governance goals, no standalone enforcement remedy, social/economic democracy.
- **Rights bind State action and sometimes private conduct**; **DPSPs guide State policy**. Both concern individual **and** collective welfare.
- “Rights negative, DPSPs positive” is a rough contrast: rights also impose positive duties, e.g. **21A**. “Rights need no legislation” is also too absolute, e.g. statutory implementation of **17/23**.
- Courts cannot strike a law down **solely** because it fails a non-justiciable DPSP, but can review it under enforceable constitutional standards. DPSP purpose informs review without replacing those standards.
- Constitutional duty under **37** is more than an optional aspiration; direct litigation remedies depend on rights/statutes and the particular constitutional provision.

## 7. Conflict and harmony: judgment timeline

- **Champakam Dorairajan 1951:** enforceable Rights prevailed in that conflict; **1st Amendment 1951** introduced protective changes. **4th 1955/17th 1964** also supported land-reform/directive implementation.
- **Golaknath 1967:** Parliament could not abridge Rights under then-view; later displaced. **24th 1971:** affirmed constituent amendment power.
- **25th 1971:** **31C** protection for laws implementing **39(b)/(c)**; originally referred to **14/19/31**, now 31 omitted.
- **Kesavananda Bharati 1973:** amend Rights subject to **basic structure**; upheld limited 31C protection but struck the clause excluding review of whether the law genuinely implements those policies.
- **42nd 1976:** attempted protection for laws implementing **all DPSPs**. **Minerva Mills 1980:** invalidated that extension; **harmony/balance between III and IV is basic structure**.
- **Operative principle:** realise welfare goals while preserving constitutional rights; no absolute supremacy of all DPSPs over all Rights. Limited **31C shield from 14/19 for genuine 39(b)/(c) laws** remains; amendments cannot destroy basic structure.
- Memory: **1951 Rights priority → 1967 amendment restriction → 1973 basic structure → 1980 balance**.

![The current rule protects constitutional balance, not unlimited primacy.](Revision%20Diagrams/cases.svg)

*The current rule protects constitutional balance, not unlimited primacy.*

## 8. Criticisms and their limits

- **No legal force:** **K.T. Shah—pious superfluities/resource-dependent cheque; Nasiruddin—New Year resolutions; T.T. Krishnamachari—dustbin of sentiments; K.C. Wheare—manifesto/moral homily; Jennings—pious aspirations**.
- **Illogical mixture:** **N. Srinivasan/Jennings** criticised arrangement/inconsistent philosophy. Response: integrated social goals can reflect multiple traditions rather than a single school.
- **Conservative/outdated:** Jennings associated them with **Fabian/Webb influences**; this is criticism, not constitutional fact that directives have expired.
- **Potential constitutional conflict:** **K. Santhanam** feared Centre–State, President–PM and Governor–CM disputes. Failure to implement a DPSP is **not by itself an automatic dismissal ground or unrestricted presidential veto**; operative constitutional powers control.
- Criticisms raise implementation/enforcement questions; they do not erase Article 37's governance duty.

## 9. Utility and political sanction

- **Alladi/Ambedkar:** responsible government must answer to electorate for ignoring directives. **L.M. Singhvi:** life-giving social-justice philosophy; **M.C. Chagla:** welfare-State ideal; **Austin:** social revolution; **B.N. Rau:** educative moral precepts.
- **M.C. Setalvad:** instructions to all authorities, judicial-review guidance, background to State action and amplification of Preamble.
- Roles: policy continuity across governments; material conditions for effective Rights; opposition scrutiny; performance yardstick; common constitutional programme transcending party manifestos.
- The **Rights–DPSP relationship is complementary**: political participation is weakened when poverty/illiteracy deny effective opportunities.

## 10. Implementation: economic and labour examples

- **Planning Commission 1950/Five-Year Plans → NITI Aayog 2015**; development/inequality goals. These institutional examples are historical policy choices, not bodies mandated by Part IV.
- Land reforms: remove intermediaries (**zamindar/jagirdar/inamdar**), tenancy security/fair rent, ceilings, surplus redistribution, cooperative farming.
- Historical labour laws: **Trade Unions 1926; Payment of Wages 1936; Minimum Wages/Factories 1948; Industrial Disputes 1947; Mines 1952; Bonus 1965; Contract Labour 1970; employee compensation 1923; Bonded Labour 1976; child-labour law 1986/2016**; maternity **1961**, equal remuneration **1976**.
- **Update:** four Labour Codes—**Wages 2019; Industrial Relations, Social Security, Occupational Safety/Health/Working Conditions 2020**—made effective **21 November 2025**, consolidating **29 laws**. Treat older chapter Acts as historical implementation examples, subject to repeal/savings/transition provisions. [Official Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)
- **Life-insurance nationalisation 1956; 14 banks 1969; privy purses abolished 1971**. General-insurance takeover began **1971**, but nationalisation Act **1972**, effective **1 January 1973**—distinguish dates. [Insurance regulator history](https://old.irdai.gov.in/ADMINCMS/cms/NormalData_Layout.aspx?page=PageNo4)

## 11. Implementation: legal aid, rural welfare and environment

- **Legal Services Authorities Act 1987:** nationwide legal-aid network/Lok Adalats. Ordinary Lok Adalat resolves through compromise, not a contested merits trial; award deemed decree, final/binding, no ordinary appeal; narrow constitutional challenge is distinct.
- Rural/cottage support: **KVIC/boards, NSIC, coir/silk/handloom/handicraft institutions**; some listed boards are historical/reorganised, not all presently active.
- Programme chronology: **Community Development 1952; Hill Area Development Programme **1974–75**; Drought-Prone Areas 1973; Minimum Needs 1974; IRDP 1978; Jawahar Rozgar 1989; SGSY 1999; SGRY 2001; rural employment guarantee implementation 2006 under 2005 Act**. Do not treat predecessor programmes as simultaneous current schemes. The chapter’s 1960 Hill Area date is corrected to the programme’s Fifth-Plan initiation. [Planning Commission study](https://digitallibrary.niti.gov.in/items/4f776fd9-c2b5-408f-a8f8-3add64f37641)
- Environment: **Wildlife Protection 1972; Forest Conservation 1980** (later renamed **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam**); **Water 1974/Air 1981**, pollution-control boards; **National Forest Policy 1988**.
- Scientific agriculture: seeds, fertilisers, irrigation and better animal-husbandry methods; public-health infrastructure and disease-control programmes; nutrition/living-standard measures.

## 12. Implementation: inclusion, local institutions and heritage

- **73rd Amendment 1992**, effective **1993:** Panchayats' constitutional status; three levels with constitutional exceptions, not every State/area forced into an identical arrangement.
- Protective measures/reservations: **Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955**, renamed **1976**; **SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989**. **65th 1990:** combined SC/ST Commission; **89th 2003:** separate NCSC/NCST.
- Commissions: **NCW 1992; NCBC statutory 1993 → constitutional 102nd 2018; NCM statutory 1993; NCPCR constituted 2007 under 2005 law**.
- **EWS 10% central scheme 2019**, enabled by **103rd**; separate from SC/ST/OBC schemes. Rights and constitutional conditions still apply.
- **Judiciary–executive separation:** criminal-procedure reforms implementing **50**; current **BNSS** replaced CrPC with savings from **July 2024**. Executive magistrate functions still exist—separation did not abolish every executive adjudicatory responsibility.
- Heritage: **1951 declaration-of-national-importance Act**; distinguish wider **Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act 1958**. [India Code](https://www.indiacode.nic.in/indiacode/bitstream/123456789/13053/2/A1958-24.pdf)
- State cattle-protection laws, social pensions and public healthcare are examples; eligibility ages vary, so the chapter's **65-year** pension illustration is not a universal rule.
- **Panchsheel/non-alignment** illustrate international-peace policy. Financial constraints, social inequality, population pressure, administrative capacity and federal coordination affect implementation.

## 13. Directives outside Part IV

- **335, Part XVI:** SC/ST service claims consistently with efficiency; constitutional proviso applies.
- **350A, Part XVII:** mother-tongue primary-instruction facilities for linguistic-minority children.
- **351, Part XVII:** Union duty to promote/develop Hindi for India's composite culture.
- Read with whole Constitution; these are **not Part IV DPSPs**, and their precise legal effect depends on their text/context rather than an automatic identical classification.

## 14. One-minute recall and mains structure

- **DPSPs non-justiciable, but fundamental in governance. Classification is scholarly.**
- **42nd: child/legal aid/workers/environment; 44th: inequalities; 86th: early childhood; 97th: cooperatives.**
- **Rights + DPSPs: means and goals; basic structure protects harmony.**
- **Mains:** constitutional goal → implementing law/programme → outcomes/remaining barriers → rights safeguards → practical reforms in funding/accountability/federal coordination.

Directive Principles of State Policy

1. Nature, origin and constitutional role

  • Part IV, 36–51: 36 defines State as in Part III; 37 states nature/duty; substantive directives mainly 38–51. Irish Constitution 1937 influence, with Spanish antecedents.
  • Ambedkar—novel features/instructions to legislature and executive; parallels the 1935 Act's Instrument of Instructions. Granville Austin: Rights + DPSPs = conscience of the Constitution.
  • Aim: welfare State, social/economic democracy and Preamble's justice/liberty/equality/fraternity; go beyond a State confined to policing and defence.
  • Not independently enforceable in court, but fundamental in governance; State has a constitutional duty to apply them in lawmaking. Political accountability/public opinion supply the principal sanction.
  • Courts use them to interpret rights and assess statutory purpose/reasonableness; implementing a DPSP does not automatically cure every constitutional violation.
  • B.N. Rau: justiciable/non-justiciable distinction. Reasons for non-justiciability: resource limits, diverse/backward conditions and flexibility over timing/priorities for the new State.

2. Socialistic principles: justice and welfare

  • 38: just social order; reduce income/status/facility/opportunity inequalities among individuals and groups.
  • 39(a): adequate livelihood for men/women equally; (b): material resources distributed for common good; (c): avoid wealth/production concentration to common detriment.
  • 39(d): equal pay for equal work; (e): protect worker health/strength and children from abuse/economic compulsion; (f): healthy development, dignity and childhood/youth protection from exploitation/abandonment.
  • 39A: equal justice/free legal aid. 41: work, education and public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness/disability and undeserved want, within economic capacity/development.
  • 42: humane working conditions and maternity relief. 43: living wage, decent life, leisure/social/cultural opportunity. 43A: worker participation in management. 47: nutrition, living standards and public health.
  • Wage distinction: minimum—basic statutory protection; fair—between minimum and living in textbook formulation; living—decent life including wider education/health/social needs. Actual wage law, not this mnemonic alone, determines entitlement.

3. Gandhian principles

  • 40: village Panchayats with self-government powers. 43: rural cottage industries on individual/cooperative basis.
  • 43B: voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control and professional cooperative management.
  • 46: weaker sections, particularly SCs/STs—education/economic interests and protection from injustice/exploitation.
  • 47: prohibit harmful intoxicating drinks/drugs except medicinal purposes. 48: preserve/improve breeds; prohibit slaughter of cows/calves and other milch/draught cattle.
  • Categories are textbook classifications, not constitutional headings; one Article can serve more than one category.

4. Liberal-intellectual principles

  • 44: Uniform Civil Code for citizens. 45: early childhood care/education below six.
  • 48: scientific agriculture/animal husbandry. 48A: environment, forests and wildlife.
  • 49: protect monuments/places/objects of artistic/historic interest declared of national importance.
  • 50: judiciary–executive separation in State public services. 51: international peace/security, just honourable relations, respect for international law/treaties, arbitration.

5. Amendment additions: high-yield sequence

  • 42nd, 1976—four changes: healthy child development 39(f); free legal aid 39A; worker management participation 43A; environment 48A.
  • 44th, 1978: minimise specified inequalities 38(2).
  • 86th, 2002: 45 changed from original under-14 education goal to below-six care/education; 21A makes 6–14 education a right; 51A(k) gives parental/guardian duty. Relevant provisions operational 2010.
  • 97th, 2011: 43B cooperatives, effective 2012. Judicial invalidation of Part IXB for State-only cooperatives does not remove 43B.

6. Rights versus DPSPs: compare without overstatement

  • Rights: enforceable constitutional guarantees, legal remedies, political democracy plus dignity/social aspects; DPSPs: governance goals, no standalone enforcement remedy, social/economic democracy.
  • Rights bind State action and sometimes private conduct; DPSPs guide State policy. Both concern individual and collective welfare.
  • “Rights negative, DPSPs positive” is a rough contrast: rights also impose positive duties, e.g. 21A. “Rights need no legislation” is also too absolute, e.g. statutory implementation of 17/23.
  • Courts cannot strike a law down solely because it fails a non-justiciable DPSP, but can review it under enforceable constitutional standards. DPSP purpose informs review without replacing those standards.
  • Constitutional duty under 37 is more than an optional aspiration; direct litigation remedies depend on rights/statutes and the particular constitutional provision.

7. Conflict and harmony: judgment timeline

  • Champakam Dorairajan 1951: enforceable Rights prevailed in that conflict; 1st Amendment 1951 introduced protective changes. 4th 1955/17th 1964 also supported land-reform/directive implementation.
  • Golaknath 1967: Parliament could not abridge Rights under then-view; later displaced. 24th 1971: affirmed constituent amendment power.
  • 25th 1971: 31C protection for laws implementing 39(b)/(c); originally referred to 14/19/31, now 31 omitted.
  • Kesavananda Bharati 1973: amend Rights subject to basic structure; upheld limited 31C protection but struck the clause excluding review of whether the law genuinely implements those policies.
  • 42nd 1976: attempted protection for laws implementing all DPSPs. Minerva Mills 1980: invalidated that extension; harmony/balance between III and IV is basic structure.
  • Operative principle: realise welfare goals while preserving constitutional rights; no absolute supremacy of all DPSPs over all Rights. Limited 31C shield from 14/19 for genuine 39(b)/(c) laws remains; amendments cannot destroy basic structure.
  • Memory: 1951 Rights priority → 1967 amendment restriction → 1973 basic structure → 1980 balance.

8. Criticisms and their limits

  • No legal force: K.T. Shah—pious superfluities/resource-dependent cheque; Nasiruddin—New Year resolutions; T.T. Krishnamachari—dustbin of sentiments; K.C. Wheare—manifesto/moral homily; Jennings—pious aspirations.
  • Illogical mixture: N. Srinivasan/Jennings criticised arrangement/inconsistent philosophy. Response: integrated social goals can reflect multiple traditions rather than a single school.
  • Conservative/outdated: Jennings associated them with Fabian/Webb influences; this is criticism, not constitutional fact that directives have expired.
  • Potential constitutional conflict: K. Santhanam feared Centre–State, President–PM and Governor–CM disputes. Failure to implement a DPSP is not by itself an automatic dismissal ground or unrestricted presidential veto; operative constitutional powers control.
  • Criticisms raise implementation/enforcement questions; they do not erase Article 37's governance duty.

9. Utility and political sanction

  • Alladi/Ambedkar: responsible government must answer to electorate for ignoring directives. L.M. Singhvi: life-giving social-justice philosophy; M.C. Chagla: welfare-State ideal; Austin: social revolution; B.N. Rau: educative moral precepts.
  • M.C. Setalvad: instructions to all authorities, judicial-review guidance, background to State action and amplification of Preamble.
  • Roles: policy continuity across governments; material conditions for effective Rights; opposition scrutiny; performance yardstick; common constitutional programme transcending party manifestos.
  • The Rights–DPSP relationship is complementary: political participation is weakened when poverty/illiteracy deny effective opportunities.

  • Planning Commission 1950/Five-Year Plans → NITI Aayog 2015; development/inequality goals. These institutional examples are historical policy choices, not bodies mandated by Part IV.
  • Land reforms: remove intermediaries (zamindar/jagirdar/inamdar), tenancy security/fair rent, ceilings, surplus redistribution, cooperative farming.
  • Historical labour laws: Trade Unions 1926; Payment of Wages 1936; Minimum Wages/Factories 1948; Industrial Disputes 1947; Mines 1952; Bonus 1965; Contract Labour 1970; employee compensation 1923; Bonded Labour 1976; child-labour law 1986/2016; maternity 1961, equal remuneration 1976.

chapters.markdown:
# Fundamental Duties

## 1. Origin and constitutional location

- Original Constitution had **Fundamental Rights and State-directed DPSPs**, but no separate Fundamental Duties list.
- **USSR influence; Swaran Singh Committee 1976; 42nd Amendment 1976 → Part IVA, Article 51A, ten duties**. **86th Amendment 2002 → eleventh educational duty, 51A(k)**.
- Committee appointed by **Congress during 1975–77 Emergency**; recommended a separate chapter and **eight duties**, while final amendment included ten.
- Unaccepted recommendations: **tax-payment duty; general penalties for non-compliance; immunity of penalty laws from constitutional challenge**. Tax duties exist under ordinary law, but paying tax is not an express 51A duty.
- Comparative caution: Japan has constitutional duties, but the chapter's claim that it is the only democracy with duties is too absolute; distinguish a named consolidated list from duties elsewhere in constitutions.

![Distinguish introduction from the later educational addition.](Revision%20Diagrams/origin.svg)

*Distinguish introduction from the later educational addition.*

## 2. All eleven duties: clause-wise recall

- **(a) Constitution and symbols:** abide by Constitution, respect ideals/institutions, National Flag and Anthem.
- **(b) Freedom struggle:** cherish/follow the noble ideals inspiring national struggle.
- **(c) Nation:** uphold/protect **sovereignty, unity, integrity**.
- **(d) Defence:** defend country and render national service **when called upon**.
- **(e) Harmony and women:** common brotherhood across religious, linguistic, regional/sectional diversity; renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity.
- **(f) Culture:** value/preserve rich heritage of **composite culture**.
- **(g) Environment:** protect/improve forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife; **compassion for living creatures**.
- **(h) Reason and reform:** scientific temper, **humanism**, inquiry and reform.
- **(i) Public property:** safeguard it and **abjure violence**.
- **(j) Excellence:** strive in individual/collective activities so nation rises in endeavour/achievement.
- **(k) Education:** citizen **parent/guardian** provides educational opportunities to child/ward **6–14**. Added **86th**, alongside **21A** and revised **45**.
- Recall groups: **Constitution–struggle–nation–defence; harmony–culture; environment–reason; property–excellence–education**.

![Recall all eleven clauses in three groups.](Revision%20Diagrams/duties.svg)

*Recall all eleven clauses in three groups.*

## 3. Nature and legal effect

- Applies to **citizens**, unlike some Rights that extend to persons/foreigners. Ordinary laws can still impose obligations on non-citizens.
- **Moral and civic:** freedom-struggle ideals are a moral example; constitutional/symbol respect a civic one; categories overlap.
- Reflect civic values, constitutional unity, dignity and inherited cultural/environmental responsibilities; not a licence to impose one religious interpretation on everyone.
- **Not independently justiciable:** no automatic constitutional punishment for every breach. Existing or valid new legislation may enforce particular obligations with penalties.
- Duties can guide interpretation/reasonableness; they do **not automatically override Rights** or exempt laws from judicial review. Legislative competence and constitutional limits still apply.
- **21A:** State's educational right obligation; **45:** State's early-childhood policy goal; **51A(k):** parent's/guardian's duty—different duty-bearers and age bands.

![Constitutional interpretation connects rights, goals and responsibilities.](Revision%20Diagrams/trinity.svg)

*Constitutional interpretation connects rights, goals and responsibilities.*

## 4. Criticisms and balanced assessment

- **Incomplete:** voting, tax payment, family planning absent from express list. Their absence does not nullify separately enacted legal obligations.
- **Vague:** noble ideals/composite culture/scientific temper can invite differing interpretations; **D.D. Chawla** called for clearer, accessible wording.
- **Non-justiciable:** criticised as moral precepts without direct sanctions. Response: educational/interpretive value and specific implementing laws.
- **Superfluous/paternalistic:** **C.K. Daphtary/A.K. Sen** questioned formal instruction to citizens and State distrust; these were political opinions, not constitutional rulings.
- **Placement:** critics preferred adjacency to Part III, rather than after Part IV. Their actual location is a separate **Part IVA**, not merely provisions within Part IV.
- Emergency-era inclusion should be assessed alongside later retention and broad civic purposes.

## 5. Significance and judicial use

- Remind citizens that public life involves responsibility alongside rights; encourage active participation, discipline, solidarity, environmental care and excellence.
- Oppose destruction of public property, violence and insults covered by lawful legislation; avoid treating every dissenting act as anti-national.
- **Mohan Kumar Singhania 1991:** duties assist interpretation of ambiguous law. **Ramlila Maidan 2012:** read **III, IV, IVA** together when assessing rights, governance and duties.
- **H.R. Gokhale/Indira Gandhi:** defended duties as promoting legal-order respect and democratic balance; retain these as historical justifications, not a rule subordinating liberty.
- **Janata Government retained duties** while undoing several Emergency amendments through **43rd 1977/44th 1978**. Addition in **2002** reinforces their continuing constitutional role.

## 6. Verma Committee 1999: existing legal support

- **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971:** Constitution, Flag, Anthem protections.
- Enmity/national-integration offences: historical **IPC**, now relevant **BNS** provisions since **July 2024**, subject to savings and offence-specific elements.
- **Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955:** untouchability-related disabilities; renamed from Untouchability (Offences) Act in **1976**. It is not a general punishment for every religious disagreement.
- **UAPA 1967:** prescribed unlawful-association framework; **Representation of the People Act 1951:** prohibited electoral appeals/corrupt practices and disqualification machinery under law.
- **Wildlife Protection Act 1972:** regulated/prohibited wildlife trade; **Forest Conservation Act 1980**, later renamed **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam**: conservation/diversion control.
- Committee identified legal support already available; **1999 did not insert the duties**, and no single Act automatically criminalises all eleven.

## 7. One-minute recall and mains structure

- **42nd → ten; 86th → eleven; Part IVA → 51A; Swaran Singh → introduction; Verma → legal support.**
- **(e) women/harmony; (g) environment/compassion; (h) science/humanism; (k) education 6–14.**
- **Mains:** origin → citizenship responsibilities → examples/laws → non-justiciability and rights safeguards → education/public participation rather than indiscriminate penalties.

[Official Constitution, Article 51A](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/c9fe9c9b6840524844316f74bb1c556c.pdf)

chapters.markdown:
# Amendment of the Constitution

## 1. Adaptability with constitutional limits

- **Part XX, Article 368:** Parliament's constituent power to amend by **addition, variation or repeal** through prescribed procedure.
- India blends **flexibility and rigidity**; changes respond to social/political needs while protecting foundational commitments.
- **Kesavananda Bharati, 24 April 1973:** amendment power is wide but cannot **damage/destroy basic structure**. An amendment to Fundamental Rights is possible; destruction of constitutional fundamentals is not.
- Distinguish **constituent amendment under 368** from ordinary legislation expressly authorised to change particular constitutional arrangements.

## 2. Article 368: complete procedure

- Introduce amendment Bill in **either House of Parliament**; **minister or private member** may introduce it. **No prior presidential recommendation** required under 368; State legislature cannot introduce it.
- Each House separately passes **majority of total membership AND at least two-thirds present and voting**. Abstentions are not votes, but total membership is not reduced by absence/vacancies.
- **No joint sitting** to resolve disagreement. Lok Sabha cannot bypass Rajya Sabha; both Houses' approval essential.
- If specified federal provisions change, ratification by legislatures of **at least half the States**, through resolutions by ordinary majority, is required **before presidential presentation**.
- **No constitutional time limit for State ratification**. Remaining States need not all respond once required threshold is reached; “half” rounds up if total odd.
- President **must assent** after valid passage/required ratification; cannot withhold or return under this procedure. **24th Amendment 1971** made the obligation express.
- Assent makes it an Act; **commencement follows its terms**—some provisions may operate on later notified dates rather than immediately on assent.

![Both parliamentary Houses and applicable ratification requirements must be satisfied.](Revision%20Diagrams/procedure.svg)

*Both parliamentary Houses and applicable ratification requirements must be satisfied.*

## 3. Special-majority calculation

- Two simultaneous tests in **each House**: **more than half total membership**; **at least two-thirds present and voting**. Use whichever requires more affirmative votes.
- Example: total **250**, present/voting **180**. Total-membership threshold **126**; two-thirds **120**; **126 yes votes needed**.
- If only **100** vote, total-membership threshold remains **126**—amendment cannot pass in that division even if every voter agrees.
- Quorum, presence and affirmative-vote thresholds are different concepts. Lok Sabha procedure applies constitutional majority requirements at effective stages, not just as an informal final tally.

![A constitutional majority combines total membership and actual votes.](Revision%20Diagrams/majority.svg)

*A constitutional majority combines total membership and actual votes.*

## 4. Route A: ordinary/simple-majority law outside 368

- **2–4:** admit/establish/reorganise States; First/Fourth Schedule consequential changes. **169:** create/abolish State Legislative Council after the State Assembly's specified **special-majority resolution**; Parliament's resulting law is ordinary legislation.
- Other authorised matters: certain **Second-Schedule payments**, parliamentary quorum, members' salaries, procedure/privileges, English use in Parliament, number of SC judges, additional SC jurisdiction, official-language arrangements, citizenship, electoral/delimitation matters and UT arrangements.
- **Fifth/Sixth Schedule amendment powers:** expressly permit parliamentary changes outside 368, subject to their terms.
- Not every law on these subjects rewrites constitutional text; not every clause mentioning salaries, language, courts or UTs is freely amendable by ordinary majority. Follow the **specific enabling provision and safeguards**.
- Ordinary-law “simple majority” generally means majority **present and voting**, subject to quorum and procedure; no 368 special-majority test for these authorised changes.

## 5. Route B: special majority of Parliament alone

- Provisions not requiring State ratification and not expressly changeable outside 368: e.g. **Fundamental Rights, DPSPs** and many other provisions.
- **Both Houses' 368 majority** required; basic-structure review applies.
- A proposal's effects can trigger ratification even if its title appears unrelated to federalism; substance matters.

## 6. Route C: special majority plus State ratification

- **President election—54/55**; **Union/State executive power—73/162**; **279A GST Council**.
- **Union judiciary:** Part V, Chapter IV; **High Courts:** Part VI, Chapter V; **legislative Union–State relations:** Part XI, Chapter I.
- **Seventh-Schedule lists; States' representation in Parliament; Article 368 itself**.
- GST-Council inclusion in the ratification proviso came with **101st Amendment 2016**.
- Ratification requirement protects specified federal arrangements; **half the States**, not every State and not a referendum.
- **Rajendra N. Shah 2021:** 97th-Amendment cooperative provisions illustrate why required State ratification cannot be omitted merely by describing a change differently.

![Choose the route by the provision and legal effect of the proposed change.](Revision%20Diagrams/routes.svg)

*Choose the route by the provision and legal effect of the proposed change.*

## 7. Criticisms and balanced responses

- **Parliament-centric:** no separate constitutional convention/Assembly; States cannot initiate a 368 amendment. **169 council resolution** is a distinct ordinary-law route, not an exception permitting States to introduce 368 Bills.
- **Limited federal consent:** most amendments need no State ratification; only **half** where required. USA ratification comparison: **three-fourths of States**, with different proposal machinery.
- **Procedural gaps:** no ratification deadline; no express constitutional answer on withdrawal of ratification; potential judicial disputes. Do not invent a settled withdrawal rule.
- **Deadlock:** no joint sitting; deliberate equal-House safeguard can also block change. Similarity to ordinary lawmaking is qualified by special majorities, ratification, assent rules and basic structure.
- Criticism of “sketchy” provisions must be balanced against operational parliamentary practice and judicial clarification.
- **K.C. Wheare:** balance of flexibility/rigidity, wise variety of procedures. **Nehru:** excessive rigidity obstructs a living nation's growth. **Ambedkar:** no claim of constitutional infallibility; amendment permitted under accessible procedures.
- Ambedkar's Canada comparison reflects the historical context, not a present claim that Canada's Constitution cannot be amended.

## 8. One-minute recall and answer structure

- **Ordinary law where expressly authorised; otherwise 368 special majority; specified federal changes add half-State ratification.**
- **Either House; private member allowed; no prior presidential recommendation; no joint sitting; mandatory assent.**
- **Two-thirds of votes alone is insufficient; also majority of total House strength.**
- **Mains:** need for change → constitutional route/majority → federal consent → basic-structure limit → evaluate adaptability versus stability.

[Official Constitution, Article 368 and amendment proviso](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/c9fe9c9b6840524844316f74bb1c556c.pdf)

Amendment of the Constitution

1. Adaptability with constitutional limits

  • Part XX, Article 368: Parliament's constituent power to amend by addition, variation or repeal through prescribed procedure.
  • India blends flexibility and rigidity; changes respond to social/political needs while protecting foundational commitments.
  • Kesavananda Bharati, 24 April 1973: amendment power is wide but cannot damage/destroy basic structure. An amendment to Fundamental Rights is possible; destruction of constitutional fundamentals is not.
  • Distinguish constituent amendment under 368 from ordinary legislation expressly authorised to change particular constitutional arrangements.

2. Article 368: complete procedure

  • Introduce amendment Bill in either House of Parliament; minister or private member may introduce it. No prior presidential recommendation required under 368; State legislature cannot introduce it.
  • Each House separately passes majority of total membership AND at least two-thirds present and voting. Abstentions are not votes, but total membership is not reduced by absence/vacancies.
  • No joint sitting to resolve disagreement. Lok Sabha cannot bypass Rajya Sabha; both Houses' approval essential.
  • If specified federal provisions change, ratification by legislatures of at least half the States, through resolutions by ordinary majority, is required before presidential presentation.
  • No constitutional time limit for State ratification. Remaining States need not all respond once required threshold is reached; “half” rounds up if total odd.

  • Two simultaneous tests in each House: more than half total membership; at least two-thirds present and voting. Use whichever requires more affirmative votes.

  • If only 100 vote, total-membership threshold remains 126—amendment cannot pass in that division even if every voter agrees.

# Basic Structure of the Constitution

## 1. Core rule

- **Article 368 permits amendment, not destruction of the Constitution's identity.** Parliament may amend any provision, including Fundamental Rights, subject to the basic structure.
- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973):** foundation of the doctrine. The Court identifies protected features through cases; there is **no exhaustive, closed list**.
- Neither every existing provision nor every policy is automatically a basic feature. Examine the amendment's **effect on constitutional fundamentals**.
- The doctrine limits **constituent power** and protects constitutional supremacy; it does not make every constitutional provision unchangeable.

![Amendment power is broad but constitutionally limited.](Revision%20Diagrams/core.svg)

*Amendment power is broad but constitutionally limited.*

## 2. Evolution: the essential chronology

- **Shankari Prasad (1951):** upheld First Amendment; “law” under 13 referred to ordinary legislation, not a constitutional amendment. Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights.
- **Sajjan Singh:** upheld Seventeenth Amendment and reaffirmed that approach. Judgment delivered **30 October 1964**, reported **1965**—the two year labels refer to the same case. Separate opinions raised doubts about altering fundamental constitutional features.
- **Golaknath (1967):** treated amendment as “law” for 13; Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights. **Prospective overruling** preserved earlier amendments.
- **24th Amendment (1971):** expressly affirmed Parliament's constituent power in 368; excluded constitutional amendments from 13; made presidential assent obligatory.
- **Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973):** overruled Golaknath's prohibition, upheld the 24th Amendment, but imposed the **basic-structure limit**.
- **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975):** invalidated **329A(4)** inserted by 39th Amendment, which insulated/validated the Prime Minister's election against the judicial process. Do not describe the whole 39th Amendment as struck down.
- **42nd Amendment (1976):** 368(4)/(5) sought to exclude amendment review and declare unlimited constituent power.
- **Minerva Mills (1980):** invalidated those clauses; **limited amending power itself is basic structure**. Also invalidated the extension of 31C protection to every DPSP; protected the balance between Parts III and IV.
- **Waman Rao (1980 decision; reported 1981):** reaffirmed the doctrine and distinguished Ninth-Schedule additions by the **24 April 1973 cutoff**.

![Follow the changing boundary of Parliament’s amendment power.](Revision%20Diagrams/timeline.svg)

*Follow the changing boundary of Parliament’s amendment power.*

## 3. Basic features: remember in five groups

- **Constitution and law:** supremacy of Constitution; rule of law; limited amending power; separation of powers; judicial review.
- **Democratic government:** sovereign, democratic, republican character; parliamentary system; free and fair elections.
- **Union and society:** federal character; unity and integrity; secular character; welfare State and socio-economic justice.
- **Person and rights:** individual freedom and dignity; equality; essence of Fundamental Rights; harmony/balance of Fundamental Rights and DPSPs.
- **Courts and remedies:** judicial independence; effective access to justice; Supreme Court powers under **32, 136, 141, 142**; High Court jurisdiction under **226, 227**.
- These are judicially recognised features, **not a separate constitutional Schedule**. Several overlap; avoid treating a mnemonic as a rigid legal taxonomy.

![Group the features for recall; the judicial list remains open.](Revision%20Diagrams/features.svg)

*Group the features for recall; the judicial list remains open.*

## 4. Case map: all chapter cases

- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973):** constitutional supremacy, separation, republican democracy, secularism, federalism, sovereignty/unity, individual dignity/freedom, welfare and parliamentary government.
- **Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975):** democracy, equality, secular freedom of conscience, rule of law, judicial review and free/fair elections.
- **Minerva Mills (1980):** limited amendment power, judicial review and FR–DPSP balance.
- **Central Coal Fields:** welfare and socio-economic justice. **Bhim Singhji:** rule of law.
- **S.P. Sampath Kumar:** judicial review; **P. Sambamurthy:** rule of law and judicial review. Read tribunal arrangements with the later **L. Chandra Kumar** ruling, not as a blanket exclusion of High Courts.
- **Delhi Judicial Service Association (1991):** Supreme Court powers under 32/136/141/142.
- **Indra Sawhney (1992):** rule of law; **Indra Sawhney II (1999):** equality. **Kumar Padma Prasad (1992):** judicial independence.
- **Kihoto Hollohan (1992):** democratic framework and free/fair elections. Its judicial-review exclusion also illustrates the separate need for **State ratification** where the federal proviso applies.
- **Raghunath Rao (1993):** equality and unity/integrity in the privy-purse abolition challenge.
- **S.R. Bommai (1994):** federalism, secularism, democracy, unity/integrity, social justice and judicial review.
- **L. Chandra Kumar (1997):** High Court review under 226/227; tribunal decisions remain subject to the constitutional courts' scrutiny.
- **All India Judges' Association:** judicial independence. **Kuldip Nayar (2006):** democracy and free/fair elections; every alteration of an electoral rule is not necessarily basic-structure destruction.
- **M. Nagaraj (2006):** equality; constitutional identity must survive an amendment.
- **I.R. Coelho (2007):** rule of law, separation, judicial review and the essence of rights; Ninth-Schedule protection is not absolute.
- **Ram Jethmalani (2011):** Article 32's remedial importance. **Namit Sharma (2012):** freedom/dignity; its specific Information Commission directions were modified on review in 2013, so do not assume every original direction remains operative.
- **Madras Bar Association (2014):** judicial review and High Court jurisdiction under 226/227; tribunal design must respect judicial independence.

## 5. Ninth Schedule: the exam distinction

- **31B** protects scheduled laws from the specified Part III invalidity; the Schedule is not an immunity from all constitutional scrutiny.
- For laws inserted **after 24 April 1973**, courts can examine whether the amendment's effect on rights damages basic structure: **Waman Rao → I.R. Coelho**.
- The cutoff concerns **insertion into the Ninth Schedule**, not merely the original date of the ordinary law.
- A Fundamental Rights violation and basic-structure destruction are related but **not automatically identical tests**.
- Ordinary legislation is ordinarily tested against constitutional provisions and legislative competence; do not mechanically apply the amendment doctrine to every statute as an independent free-standing test.

## 6. One-minute recall / Mains frame

- **1951/1964–65: amend Rights allowed → 1967: prohibited → 1971: constituent power express → 1973: amend, but preserve basic structure → 1980: unlimited-power claim rejected.**
- **No Article expressly lists basic structure; its foundation is judicial interpretation of amendment power.**
- Mains: need for constitutional change → limited constituent power → key cases/features → democracy, federalism and rights protected → concern about judicial discretion → reasoned, case-specific scrutiny.

[Supreme Court's Kesavananda Bharati judgment resource](https://judgments.ecourts.gov.in/KBJ/?p=home%2Fbackground)
[National Judicial Academy: basic structure case chronology](https://www.nja.gov.in/Concluded_Programmes/2018-19/SE-02_2018_PPTs/1.Basic%20structure%20of%20constitution.pdf)
