← Study home

Centre-State Relations

1. Three dimensions of federal relations

  • Legislative: who makes the law? Administrative: who implements it? Financial: who taxes, receives revenue and borrows?
  • Division of legislative, executive and financial authority coexists with an integrated judiciary enforcing Union and State laws. Both governments have constitutionally protected spheres; coordination makes them work together.
  • Core provisions: legislative relations 245-255, administrative relations 256-263 (Part XI); financial relations mainly 268-293 (Part XII). Other provisions also apply.

2. Legislative relations: territory and subjects

  • 245: Parliament legislates for all/part of India, including States, UTs and acquired territory. State law operates within its State; an outside connection requires sufficient territorial nexus. A parliamentary law is not invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation.
  • Territorial qualifications: Presidential regulations for Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu; Puducherry when its Assembly is dissolved/suspended as specified under 240. Ladakh regulations are provided for by section 58(2), J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019, using Article 240. Such regulations can amend/repeal parliamentary laws applicable there.
  • Fifth Schedule: Governor may exclude/modify parliamentary or State Acts in Scheduled Areas. Sixth Schedule: special application/modification rules operate in autonomous tribal areas; chapter highlights Governor's role in Assam and President's role in Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. These are specific constitutional exceptions, not blanket exclusion of Parliament.
  • 246 + Seventh Schedule: Union List = national importance/uniformity; State List = local/regional interests; Concurrent List = shared interests permitting uniformity with diversity.
  • Union examples: defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency, atomic energy, insurance, communications, inter-State trade, census, audit. State examples: public order, police, public health, agriculture, prisons, local government, fisheries, markets, theatres, gambling. Concurrent examples: criminal/civil procedure, marriage/divorce, population control, electricity, labour welfare, economic/social planning, drugs, newspapers and books.
  • Entry counts: original 97 Union / 66 State / 47 Concurrent; chapter's current operative count 98 / 59 / 52. Numbering retains gaps and lettered additions: last serial number is not the active-entry total. Union additions 2A, 92A, 92B; omissions 33, 92, 92C. State omissions 11, 19, 20, 29, 36, 52, 55. Concurrent additions 11A, 17A, 17B, 20A, 33A.
  • 42nd Amendment, 1976: five transfers to Concurrent List: education; forests; weights and measures; protection of wild animals/birds; administration of justice and organisation of courts except SC/HCs. Remember E-F-W-W-J.
  • 246(4): Parliament can legislate on State List matters for territory not included in a State, notably UTs, subject to applicable special arrangements.
  • 248: Parliament holds residuary legislative/tax powers, subject to 246A. GST has a special constitutional distribution: both levels legislate; inter-State GST exclusively Parliament.
  • Comparative recall: USA/Australia leave residual authority broadly with States; Canada with Centre. Government of India Act, 1935: three lists, but residual allocation by Governor-General; present India combines three lists with parliamentary residuary authority.

3. Legislative priority and repugnancy

  • Under 246, Union competence prevails over competing State/Concurrent competence; Concurrent over State, subject to constitutional interpretation and reconciliation of entries.
  • 254: repugnancy between valid Union and State laws on a Concurrent subject ordinarily makes the State law void to the extent of conflict.
  • 254(2) exception: State law reserved for and assented to by President may prevail in that State over the specified earlier parliamentary/existing law; Parliament may later override it. Presidential assent does not cure every constitutional defect.
  • 251: parliamentary laws under 249/250 prevail over inconsistent State laws while they operate; the State law is inoperative to the extent of repugnancy for that period.
  • Do not confuse overlapping legislative entries, Concurrent-list repugnancy, and GST's special 246A framework.

4. Five routes for Parliament to legislate in the State field

  • 249 - National interest: Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds present and voting; valid up to one year, renewable up to one year at a time. Resulting law ceases to operate six months after resolution expires. State legislative competence continues; Union law prevails on conflict. Provision also expressly covers GST.
  • 250 - National Emergency: Parliament can legislate on State List matters/GST while 352 operates; law ceases six months after Emergency ends. States can still legislate; Union law prevails on conflict.
  • 252 - State request: resolutions by legislatures of two or more States (both Houses where bicameral); parliamentary law applies to requesting States, and others may later adopt it. Only Parliament can amend/repeal it under the Article's procedure. A single State alone cannot initiate this route; consenting States surrender legislative control over the covered matter.
  • 253 - International obligations: Parliament may implement treaties, agreements, conventions and international decisions, including on State subjects; State consent is not a constitutional prerequisite.
  • 356/357 - President's Rule: State legislative authority becomes exercisable by/under Parliament. Laws continue after President's Rule until competent authority changes them; State legislature can subsequently alter/repeal them.
  • 252 examples: Prize Competitions Act 1955; Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972; Water Act 1974; Urban Land Ceiling Act 1976; Transplantation of Human Organs Act 1994. Wildlife later moved to Concurrent List; these examples describe their enactment context.
  • 253 examples: Geneva Conventions Act 1960; environment/TRIPS legislation; historical Anti-Hijacking Act 1982 (replaced by 2016 Act). UN Privileges and Immunities Act 1947 predates the Constitution: international-obligation example, not literally enacted under Article 253.

5. Union influence over State legislation

  • 200/201: Governor may reserve a State Bill for President; President can assent/withhold assent and direct reconsideration of a non-Money Bill. The State legislature has six months to reconsider after receiving the President's message. Do not treat veto labels as a licence for arbitrary inaction.
  • 304(b): Bills imposing specified reasonable restrictions on inter-State/within-State trade in public interest require prior presidential sanction for introduction/moving amendment. Not every State tax Bill falls under this clause.
  • 213: certain ordinances need presidential instructions: where equivalent Bill needs prior presidential sanction, would have been reserved, or would be invalid without presidential assent.
  • 360: financial-emergency directions may require reservation of Money Bills and other Bills to which 207 applies, after State legislature passes them.
  • Sarkaria's rationale: Union supremacy resolves conflicts and preserves workable, coherent legislation; it should coexist with consultation and protected State spheres.
  • Assent update (2025): the Supreme Court's Presidential Reference opinion rejects judicially fixed assent deadlines/deemed assent; prolonged, unexplained Governor inaction can attract limited judicial direction to decide. Punchhi's proposed six-month Governor/President deadline is a recommendation, not a general enacted constitutional rule. Supreme Court opinion.

6. Administrative relations: execution and directions

  • 73/162: executive authority generally follows legislative competence. Union executes Union subjects and treaty-based rights/authority; States execute State subjects.
  • Concurrent subjects: execution normally rests with States unless Constitution/parliamentary law expressly confers Union executive power. A Central law does not automatically mean exclusive Central implementation; Essential Commodities Act illustrates statutory Union powers.
  • 256: State executive must ensure compliance with applicable parliamentary/existing laws; Union may give necessary directions.
  • 257: State executive must not impede/prejudice Union executive power. Union may direct construction/maintenance of communications of national/military importance and railway protection; extra costs are dealt with constitutionally.
  • Other directions: 350A mother-tongue facilities at primary stage for linguistic-minority children; 339(2) specified Scheduled Tribe welfare schemes.
  • 365: failure to comply with constitutional Union directions may support a finding of constitutional breakdown; 356 is not automatic, and constitutional safeguards/judicial review apply.

7. Executive delegation: consent matters

  • 258(1): Union → State: President entrusts Union executive functions to State government/officers with State government's consent, conditionally/unconditionally.
  • 258(2): parliamentary law → State: Parliament may confer powers/impose duties on State government/officers even on matters beyond State legislative competence; State consent not required for this statutory route. Compensation for additional administrative costs is addressed by 258(3).
  • 258A: State → Union: Governor entrusts State executive functions to Union government/officers with Union government's consent, conditionally/unconditionally. Inserted by 7th Amendment, 1956.
  • States have no matching general unilateral statutory route to impose executive duties on Union. Executive entrustment ≠ transfer of constitutional legislative competence. Article 252 is a distinct legislative mechanism.

8. Cooperation, services and courts

  • 262: Parliament provides adjudication of inter-State river/water disputes and may exclude SC/other court jurisdiction as specified.
  • 263: President establishes Inter-State Council when public interest warrants; Council established 1990. Discuss common interests, investigate/discuss disputes, recommend coordination; distinguish this from a court's binding adjudication.
  • 261: full faith and credit to public acts, records and judicial proceedings; final civil judgments/orders executable throughout India according to law.
  • 307: Parliament may appoint authority for implementing 301-304; chapter notes no such authority. Punchhi proposed a Trade and Commerce Commission - proposal, not an existing constitutional commission.
  • All-India Services: IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service (IFoS); Centre recruits/trains, Union and States share control, officers serve at both levels. IAS/IPS succeed ICS/Indian Police and are constitutionally recognised; IFoS established 1966. Avoid confusion with Indian Foreign Service, a Central service.
  • 312: new AIS requires Rajya Sabha's two-thirds present and voting national-interest resolution, followed by parliamentary law. Common standards, strategic posts, coordination and mobility balance concern about State autonomy/patronage; AIS are constitutionally authorised, not unconstitutional merely because centralising.
  • State PSC: Governor appoints chair/members; President removes under 317, with prescribed SC inquiry where applicable. Joint State PSC: Parliament creates on concerned State legislatures' request; President appoints. UPSC: may serve State needs at Governor's request with President's approval; assists joint recruitment schemes when two or more States request.
  • Integrated courts: SC → HCs → subordinate courts; enforce both levels' laws. President appoints HC judges under constitutional process/collegium practice; transfers under 222; removal requires parliamentary special-majority address. Common HCs may be established by Parliament: Punjab/Haryana, Bombay HC for Maharashtra/Goa.
  • 355: Union duty to protect every State against external aggression/internal disturbance and ensure constitutional government. Governor is appointed by President, holds office during presidential pleasure subject to constitutional limits; constitutional head also provides Union-State link.
  • State Election Commissioner - 243K: Governor appoints; removal only in like manner/on like grounds as an HC judge. Not a simple discretionary presidential removal; service conditions cannot be varied to disadvantage after appointment.

9. Administrative emergencies and consultation forums

  • National Emergency (352/353): Union can give directions regarding State executive exercise on any matter; State governments are not automatically suspended.
  • President's Rule (356): President may assume State governmental functions/Governor or other executive powers as provided; HC powers cannot be assumed.
  • Financial Emergency (360): financial-propriety directions; reductions in salaries/allowances of specified classes serving State; Bill-reservation directions.
  • Non-constitutional ≠ non-statutory: executive/advisory examples include NITI Aayog, National Integration Council, Central health/family-welfare and local-government councils, Transport Development Council; Zonal Councils, North-Eastern Council and UGC have statutory foundations.
  • Chapter's Central Council of Indian Medicine/Homoeopathy examples are historical: replaced by NCISM (11 June 2021) and NCH (5 July 2021). NCISM · NCH.
  • Consultation conferences: Governors-President; Chief Ministers-PM; Chief Secretaries-Cabinet Secretary; police chiefs; Chief Justices-CJI; Vice-Chancellors; State Home Ministers-Union Home Minister; Law Ministers-Union Law Minister. Frequency need not be annual.

10. Fiscal powers: levy, collect and appropriate

  • Tax authority ≠ collection ≠ receipt of proceeds. Example: Union income tax collected centrally, eligible net proceeds shared with States.
  • Union/State Lists contain distinct tax entries; Concurrent List contains no tax entries. GST concurrency arises separately under 246A, not from a Concurrent tax entry. Residuary taxing power rests with Parliament.
  • Chapter groups 13 Union and 18 State tax/fee entries; entries include fees, so these are not totals of taxes currently levied. Historical gift/wealth/expenditure taxes illustrate residuary taxation, not a list of current levies.
  • 276: professions/trades/callings/employment tax capped at ₹2,500 per person per year; 60th Amendment, 1988 raised the original ₹250 cap.
  • 286: State cannot tax supplies outside State or in import/export; Parliament determines principles. 287: electricity consumed by/sold to Union, or specified railway purposes, enjoys constitutional protection subject to parliamentary law.
  • 288: State tax on water/electricity connected with parliamentary inter-State river/valley authorities requires the specified presidential-assent safeguard.
  • 80th Amendment, 2000: expanded sharing of Union taxes; linked to 10th FC alternative devolution scheme effective 1 April 1996, historically 29%; omitted 272. These are historical, not current devolution figures.
  • 101st Amendment, 2016: GST constitutional framework; inserted 246A/269A/279A, omitted 268A and Union Entry 92C (service-tax provisions inserted by 88th Amendment). GST began 1 July 2017.
  • GST absorbed Central excise/additional excise where applicable, service tax, additional customs duties (CVD/SAD), related cesses/surcharges; State VAT/sales taxes where applicable, Central sales tax, octroi/entry/purchase/luxury taxes, specified entertainment/lottery/betting/gambling taxes and related levies. It did not abolish every indirect tax: alcohol for human consumption excluded; specified petroleum products await GST commencement as constitutionally provided; basic customs duty remains.

11. Six revenue channels

  • 268 - Union levies; States collect and keep: specified stamp duties, e.g. bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, insurance policies, share transfers. In UTs, Union collects; State proceeds are assigned to that State, outside CFI.
  • 269 - Union levies/collects; States receive: specified inter-State sale/purchase and consignment taxes, except 269A; allocation by parliamentary principles. Relevant non-GST taxes must not be confused with IGST.
  • 269A - Inter-State GST: Union levies/collects; apportioned Union-State by parliamentary law on GST Council recommendations. Imports deemed inter-State supplies; Parliament determines place-of-supply/inter-State principles.
  • 270 - Divisible pool: shareable Union taxes/duties and specified Union GST proceeds, excluding 268/269/269A categories, 271 surcharges and specific-purpose cesses; President prescribes distribution on FC recommendations.
  • 271 - Union surcharge: Union retains; cannot surcharge GST under 246A. Cesses and surcharges reduce the shareable base; 41% means share of divisible pool, not all gross Union tax receipts.
  • State-own revenue: State List levies retained by States plus State GST under special framework. Examples: land revenue, agricultural-income tax; succession/estate duties on agricultural land; lands/buildings; mineral rights subject to parliamentary limitations; specified excise; electricity; petroleum/alcohol sales; road/inland-waterway goods/passengers; vehicles; animals/boats; tolls; profession tax; capitation; local-body entertainment taxes; specified stamp duties; fees excluding court fees. Constitutional competence does not imply every listed levy is currently collected.
  • Non-tax revenue examples: Union-posts, railways, broadcasting, currency-related receipts, public enterprises, escheat/lapse; States-irrigation, forests, fisheries, State enterprises, escheat/lapse. Modern receipts include fees, dividends and interest; the chapter's examples are illustrative, not a revenue ranking.

12. Grants, Finance Commission and GST Council

  • 275 - statutory grants: States needing assistance; amounts may differ; charged on CFI. Specific support for Scheduled Tribe welfare/Scheduled Area administration, including constitutional Assam provisions. FC recommends principles; not equal automatic grants to every State.
  • 282 - discretionary public-purpose grants: Union and States may grant even outside their legislative fields; supports programmes/cooperation. Textbook planning terminology is historical; constitutional power continues.
  • 273 - historical jute grants: Assam, Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal in lieu of export-duty share; limited transitional period ending by 1960, not a continuing current grant scheme.
  • 280 - Finance Commission: President constitutes every fifth year or earlier; chair + four members. Constitutionally constituted advisory body with inquiry/civil-court powers under law, often described as quasi-judicial; recommendations are not court decrees.
  • FC functions: vertical sharing Union-State; horizontal State shares; grant principles; augment State Consolidated Funds for Panchayats/Municipalities based on State FC recommendations; other presidential references for sound finance. Local-body functions followed 73rd/74th Amendments.
  • 281: recommendations plus explanatory memorandum on action taken laid before both parliamentary Houses. FC is the fiscal federalism balancing wheel, not the GST Council.
  • Devolution update: 14th FC 42% (2015-20); 15th FC 41% (2020-26); 16th FC 41% (2026-31), retained and accepted by Government. These are period-specific divisible-pool shares. Government acceptance of 16th FC recommendation.
  • 279A - GST Council: President constituted; Union Finance Minister chairs; Union Minister of State for Revenue/Finance and each State's nominated Finance/Taxation/other Minister. State members choose a Vice-Chair. Quorum half members; decision ≥three-fourths weighted votes present/voting; Union one-third weight, States together two-thirds.
  • Recommendations cover subsumed taxes/cesses/surcharges; taxable/exempt supplies; model laws, levy, IGST allocation/place of supply; turnover exemptions; rates/floor bands; special temporary disaster rates; special-category provisions and other GST matters. Council recommendations do not themselves enact tax law.

13. State safeguards, borrowing and tax immunity

  • 274: prior presidential recommendation for specified Bills/amendments affecting State-interested taxes/duties, agricultural-income definition, distribution principles or Union surcharges.
  • 279: net proceeds = gross receipts minus collection costs; CAG certifies, certificate final.
  • 292: Union may borrow domestically/abroad against CFI and give guarantees within parliamentary limits. 293: States borrow within India, against State Consolidated Fund, within State-law limits.
  • Union may lend to/guarantee State loans. State needs Union consent while Union loan/Union-guaranteed loan remains outstanding; consent may have conditions. This is not a requirement for Union permission for every State borrowing in all circumstances.
  • 285: Union property exempt from State/local taxes, subject to constitutional exceptions and parliamentary law; separate Union-owned companies/corporations do not automatically inherit immunity.
  • 289: State property/income exempt from Union taxation; Parliament may tax State commercial activity, and declare specified activities incidental to ordinary government functions. Local authorities/State companies do not automatically receive State immunity.
  • Sea Customs reference, 1963: 289 immunity does not generally exempt customs/excise duties on goods; distinguish direct property/income taxes from indirect duties.
  • 354 + National Emergency: President may modify operation of 268-279 revenue distribution, with order laid before both Houses; modifications extend no later than end of financial year in which Emergency ceases. 360: financial propriety, salary reductions, reservation of specified financial Bills.

14. Trends and friction points

  • Before 1967: common party control often eased coordination. 1967: Congress lost power in nine States; opposition governments pressed for autonomy/resources. Party competition, coalition/regional politics and fiscal dependence changed bargaining.
  • Political/constitutional friction: Governor appointment/removal/partisanship; misuse of 356; Central-force deployment; reservation/delay of State Bills; Union intrusion on State subjects; inquiries against Chief Ministers; political use of electronic media.
  • Administrative friction: AIS management; CBI/ED and other Central agencies' operation; execution of Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
  • Fiscal friction: discretionary allocations, revenue sharing, scheme burdens, borrowing controls; historical Planning Commission approval of State projects. NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission in 2015; do not transfer every old funding function to NITI.

15. Early reform initiatives: proposals versus existing law

  • First ARC (1966; report 1969): six members; Morarji Desai, later K. Hanumanthaiya; Centre-State study team M.C. Setalvad; 22 recommendations. Inter-State Council, experienced non-partisan Governors, maximum executive delegation, greater State resources, Central-force deployment with/without request. Textbook's “no action” describes early response; Council was later established.
  • Rajamannar Committee (1969; report 1971): Tamil Nadu DMK government; chair P.V. Rajamannar, members A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar and P. Chandra Reddy. Diagnosed special Union powers, one-party dominance, fiscal dependence and central planning as centralising causes.
  • Rajamannar proposals: immediate ISC; permanent FC; statutory body replacing Planning Commission; delete 356/357/365; remove ministry's Governor-pleasure provision; shift selected Union/Concurrent subjects to States; State residual powers; abolish AIS. Not adopted as a constitutional package.
  • Anandpur Sahib Resolution, 1973: Akali Dal; political/religious demands. Restrict Centre to defence, foreign affairs, communications, currency; residual powers to States; real federalism and equal State authority/representation. Demand, not constitutional change.
  • West Bengal memorandum, 1977: replace “Union” with “federal”; Centre-defence, foreign affairs, currency, communications, economic coordination; other/residual subjects to States; repeal 356/357/360; binding State consent to reorganisation; 75% total Central revenue to States; stronger Rajya Sabha; abolish AIS. Not accepted; 75% demand is not today's tax-sharing rate.

16. Sarkaria Commission: strong Centre, cooperative practice

  • 1983-88: chair R.S. Sarkaria; B. Sivaraman, S.R. Sen; 247 recommendations. Existing constitutional structure broadly sound; focus operational reform. Strong Centre necessary for unity; strength ≠ over-centralisation.
  • Institutions: permanent Inter-Governmental Council under 263; reactivate Zonal Councils; rename/reconstitute NDC as National Economic and Development Council; strengthen/create AIS; activate linguistic-minorities commissioner.
  • Autonomy safeguards: 356 last resort; consult States on Concurrent laws; communicate reasons when President withholds assent; constitutionally prescribe CM consultation on Governor appointment; protect Governor's five-year tenure except compelling reasons; no dismissal of ministry retaining Assembly majority; State-minister inquiry commissions only on parliamentary demand.
  • Competence: residual taxes stay Union, other residual powers to Concurrent; retain Union State-reorganisation power and existing Rajya Sabha role; Central armed-force deployment possible without consent but State consultation desirable.
  • Finance/planning: share corporation-tax proceeds; income-tax surcharge only specific purpose/limited time; maintain then-existing FC/Planning Commission division. Corporation tax now participates in divisible pool after 80th Amendment; planning proposals retain historical context.
  • Language/media: implement three-language formula; operational decentralisation of radio/TV rather than autonomous institutions.
  • Chapter reports 180/247 implemented; treat as its reported tally, not an independently updated count. Key institutional outcome: Inter-State Council, 1990.

17. Punchhi Commission: practical cooperative federalism

  • 2007-10: chair M.M. Punchhi, former CJI; members Dhirendra Singh, V.K. Duggal, N.R. Madhava Menon, Amaresh Bagchi (after death, Vijay Shanker joined 2008). Report seven volumes, 1,456 pages; over 310 recommendations; drew on Sarkaria, NCRWC, Second ARC. Guiding idea: cooperation supports unity, integrity and development.
  • Legislation/treaties (recommendations 1-7): broad Union-State agreement before Concurrent laws; more State flexibility on State/transferred Concurrent subjects; Union intervention only for demonstrated national uniformity; continuing ISC audit of overlap; six-month presidential assent decision; law structuring treaty-making/implementation; treaty-related State fiscal obligations in FC terms of reference.
  • Governor appointment/tenure (8-12): eminent outsider, detached from local politics, not recently politically active; fixed five years with protection against arbitrary removal; impeachment mechanism analogous to President; 163 discretion narrow, reasoned/good-faith; six-month Bill decision. Proposed impeachment/fixed deadlines are not current general constitutional provisions.
  • Hung House convention (13): widest support; majority pre-poll alliance treated as one. Suggested preference if no clear majority: largest pre-poll group → largest single party with support → post-poll coalition with all partners in government → post-poll alliance with outside supporters. Democratic majority must ultimately be tested on floor.
  • Governor's conduct (14-16): floor test before CM dismissal; prosecution sanction despite Cabinet advice if refusal demonstrably biased against overwhelming evidence; end Governor's routine university chancellorship/other statutory roles. These are reform recommendations, not blanket rules adopted everywhere.
  • Emergency safeguards (17-19): exhaust 355 alternatives; 356 only constitutional-machinery failure; incorporate Bommai 1994 safeguards; legal/constitutional framework for localised emergency while State government/Assembly continue. No new general local-emergency category was thereby created.
  • Federal institutions (20-26): strengthen 263 ISC; Zonal Councils meet at least twice yearly and use strengthened ISC secretariat; sectoral State coordination/rotating CM forum; new health, education, engineering, judicial AIS; strengthen Rajya Sabha's State voice and equal State seats through amendment; constitutionally clarify local-body devolution.
  • Fiscal accountability (27-33): Union cost-sharing in laws implemented by States (RTE model); mineral royalty revision at least every three years/compensate delays; remove profession-tax cap; review 268 revenue potential; independent annual fiscal assessments tabled in legislatures; States involved in even-handed FC terms; reduce cesses/surcharges' share.
  • Planning/commerce (34-38): examine plan/non-plan distinction; align FC/Plan cycles; permanent FC secretariat via Finance Ministry unit; Planning Commission to coordinate rather than micromanage; Trade & Commerce Commission under 307 + Union Entry 42 with advisory/executive decisions and SC appeal. Planning Commission/Five-Year Plan context is historical; plan/non-plan budget distinction ended in 2017-18 (Budget reform).
  • Standing Committee of ISC considered recommendations in 2017/2018; circulated to States for comments as reported in the chapter's MHA 2021-22 account. Recommendation ≠ enactment ≠ implementation.

18. One-minute recall and Mains structure

  • 249: RS two-thirds present/voting → ≤1 year → law lasts six months more. 250: Emergency → six months more. 252: two+ States → only Parliament amends. 253: international obligations. 356/357: laws survive restoration.
  • 258: President + State consent; 258(2): parliamentary statute without consent; 258A: Governor + Union consent.
  • 268 keep; 269 assign; 269A apportion IGST; 270 share pool; 271 Union surcharge. 275 statutory; 282 discretionary; 280 FC; 279A GST Council.
  • Sarkaria: retain structure, improve operation. Punchhi: cooperative practice, restrained Union intervention, stronger institutions and fiscal responsibility. Rajamannar: extensive State-autonomy demands.
  • Mains answer: constitutional division → specific friction (Governor, fiscal base, agencies, overlapping laws) → safeguard/example → Sarkaria/Punchhi reform → consultation, predictable transfers, floor tests and accountable implementation.
  • Prelims traps: law-making and execution differ; consent rules differ; all three crisis routes have different continuation rules; AIS ≠ Foreign Service; non-constitutional can be statutory; commissions' proposals are not automatic law.

Constitutional references

  • Official Constitution: Parts XI/XII and related provisions.
  • J&K Reorganisation Act: Ladakh regulations, section 58.

chapters.markdown:
# Inter-State Relations

## 1. Four constitutional links

- **262:** water-dispute adjudication. **263:** councils for discussion/cooperation. **261:** recognition of public acts, records and judicial proceedings. **301-307, Part XIII:** trade, commerce and intercourse.
- **Zonal Councils:** statutory regional forums under **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**; additional to constitutional mechanisms. Cooperation between States is as important as Centre-State cooperation.

![Choose the mechanism according to the issue.](Revision%20Diagrams/mechanisms.svg)

*Choose the mechanism according to the issue.*

## 2. Water disputes: advice versus adjudication

- **262:** Parliament may provide adjudication of disputes about use/distribution/control of inter-State river/valley waters and exclude SC/other court jurisdiction as specified.
- **River Boards Act, 1956:** Union establishes advisory boards for inter-State river/valley regulation and development after the prescribed consultation/request process. **Board advises; tribunal adjudicates.**
- **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956:** Union establishes tribunal where negotiation cannot settle dispute; published decision final/binding under statute. Court-jurisdiction exclusion concerns the specified water dispute; **do not infer that every constitutional challenge, implementation question or appeal is categorically outside SC scrutiny**.
- **Tribunals in chapter - constitution year and parties at that time:** Krishna I **1969** - Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh; Godavari **1969** - Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP, MP, Odisha; Narmada **1969** - Rajasthan, Gujarat, MP, Maharashtra.
- Ravi-Beas **1986** - Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan; Cauvery **1990** - Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry; Krishna II **2004** - Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP.
- Vansadhara **2010** - Odisha/AP; Mahadayi **2010** - Goa/Karnataka/Maharashtra; Mahanadi **2018** - Odisha/Chhattisgarh. **Historical constitution table, not a list of tribunals all currently active**; State reorganisation changes parties, notably Telangana in Krishna matters.

## 3. Article 263 councils and the Inter-State Council

- President establishes council if public interest served; specifies duties, organisation and procedure. Possible functions: **inquire/advise on disputes; investigate/discuss common interests; recommend coordinated policy/action**.
- **Advisory council ≠ court:** SC **131** decides qualifying inter-government legal disputes; council can discuss legal/non-legal issues but recommendations are not binding judicial decrees.
- Chapter's subject-specific examples: Central Council of Health/Family Welfare; Local Government Council (earlier Local Self-Government, 1954); four regional sales-tax councils. Distinguish historical coordination arrangements from today's GST institutions.
- **Inter-State Council Order, 28 May 1990:** V.P. Singh government acted on Sarkaria's recommendation; proposed name “Inter-Governmental Council” was not adopted. Council's established duties focus common interests, coordinated policy/action and other matters referred by chair.
- **Chair PM; members:** State CMs; CMs of UTs with Assemblies; administrators of UTs without Assemblies; Governors where President's Rule operates; **six nominated Union Cabinet Ministers**, including Home Minister. Additional permanent invitees depend on reconstitution order; chapter lists five, not an immutable constitutional number.
- Recommendatory forum; meetings in camera; consensus; provision to meet at least **three times yearly** is not proof this frequency was achieved.
- **Standing Committee, 1996:** continuous consultation, processing issues; Union Home Minister chairs; chapter composition **five other Union Cabinet Ministers + nine CMs**, subject to notified reconstitution.
- **ISC Secretariat, 1991:** headed by Secretary to Government of India; also serves Zonal Councils since **2011**.

## 4. Full faith and credit - Article 261

- India-wide recognition of **public acts, records and judicial proceedings** of Union/States. Public acts include legislative/executive acts; public records include official records made by public servants.
- Parliament prescribes proof, conditions and effect; recognition does not make every State law territorially operative throughout India.
- **Final civil judgments/orders** executable anywhere in India according to law, without a fresh suit on judgment. This specific execution clause is about **civil**, not criminal, judgments; not an absence of national criminal-law enforcement.

## 5. Trade freedom and permitted restrictions

- **301:** free trade, commerce and intercourse across India, including **inter-State and intra-State**; aim a common economic space. Regulatory measures and all taxes are not automatically prohibited restrictions.
- **302:** Parliament restricts in **public interest**. **303:** neither level ordinarily gives State preference/discrimination through trade entries; Parliament's **scarcity-of-goods exception** permitted by 303(2).
- **304(a):** State can tax imported goods if similar local goods bear same treatment; **no discrimination against imports from other States/UTs**.
- **304(b):** State can impose **reasonable public-interest restrictions**; introduction/moving amendment requires **prior presidential sanction**. Distinguish clause (a)'s non-discriminatory tax from clause (b)'s trade restrictions.
- **305:** saves specified existing laws and State-monopoly laws within constitutional conditions. Government trade/business/industry/service may exclude private participation wholly/partly.
- **307:** Parliament may create implementation authority for **301-304**; chapter notes none created. Its US Inter-State Commerce Commission comparison is historical, not a statement that that US body still exists.

![Parallel constitutional powers and limits.](Revision%20Diagrams/trade.svg)

*Parallel constitutional powers and limits.*

## 6. Five Zonal Councils

- **Statutory, advisory/deliberative:** States Reorganisation Act, 1956; no judicial enforcement power. Zones reflect geography, rivers/communications, cultural/linguistic affinity, economic development, security and law/order.
- **Union Home Minister chairs all five**; CMs act as Vice-Chair by rotation for **one year**. Members: CMs + **two other Ministers from each State**, UT administrator as provided. Advisors without vote: nominated planning/policy representative, chief secretaries, development commissioners; NITI-associated participation reflects current institutional practice.
- **Northern - New Delhi:** Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Delhi, Chandigarh, J&K, Ladakh. **Central - Prayagraj:** UP, Uttarakhand, MP, Chhattisgarh.
- **Eastern - Kolkata:** Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal. **Western - Mumbai:** Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, merged UT Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.
- **Southern - Chennai:** AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry. Newer official meetings also include **Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep**; textbook lists/older MHA webpages can be incomplete. Headquarters in the chapter are conventional zonal locations; the common Secretariat is in Delhi.
- Objectives: national/emotional integration; curb divisive regionalism/linguism; smooth reorganisation's after-effects; exchange experience; coordinate social/economic policy and major development projects; balance regional interests.
- Subjects: economic/social planning, linguistic minorities, borders, inter-State transport and other shared concerns. **Boundary issue discussed ≠ council can unilaterally redraw boundaries**.

## 7. North-Eastern Council

- **Separate statutory council:** NEC Act **1971**, operational **8 August 1972**; not a sixth Zonal Council under the 1956 Act.
- Eight States: **Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Sikkim**; Sikkim added by **2002 amendment**.
- Regional planning/coordination and review of development; textbook security/public-order description reflects original functions. **2002 amendment made NEC the regional planning body**; do not copy superseded functions as its current statutory mandate without qualification.

## 8. One-minute recall / Mains

- **262 tribunal; 263 council; 261 recognition; 301 freedom. ISC = constitutional basis/PM; Zonal = 1956 statute/Home Minister; NEC = 1971 separate statute/eight States.**
- **304(a): non-discriminatory tax; 304(b): reasonable restriction + prior presidential sanction. Council advice ≠ binding tribunal/court decision.**
- Mains: dispute/problem → constitutional mechanism → delays/implementation/cooperation challenge → negotiation, reliable data, effective institutions and accountable compliance.

## References

- [Official Constitution: Articles 261-263 and Part XIII](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/359f70a69695affb9d72f8393102bd2e.pdf).
- [MHA annual report: Southern Zonal Council participation](https://www.mha.gov.in/web/sites/default/files/AnnualReport202122_24112022%5B1%5D.pdf).

  • Inter-State Council Order, 28 May 1990: V.P. Singh government acted on Sarkaria's recommendation; proposed name “Inter-Governmental Council” was not adopted. Council's established duties focus common interests, coordinated policy/action and other matters referred by chair.
  • Chair PM; members: State CMs; CMs of UTs with Assemblies; administrators of UTs without Assemblies; Governors where President's Rule operates; six nominated Union Cabinet Ministers, including Home Minister. Additional permanent invitees depend on reconstitution order; chapter lists five, not an immutable constitutional number.
  • Recommendatory forum; meetings in camera; consensus; provision to meet at least three times yearly is not proof this frequency was achieved.
  • Standing Committee, 1996: continuous consultation, processing issues; Union Home Minister chairs; chapter composition five other Union Cabinet Ministers + nine CMs, subject to notified reconstitution.
  • ISC Secretariat, 1991: headed by Secretary to Government of India; also serves Zonal Councils since 2011.

4. Full faith and credit - Article 261

  • India-wide recognition of public acts, records and judicial proceedings of Union/States. Public acts include legislative/executive acts; public records include official records made by public servants.
  • Parliament prescribes proof, conditions and effect; recognition does not make every State law territorially operative throughout India.
  • Final civil judgments/orders executable anywhere in India according to law, without a fresh suit on judgment. This specific execution clause is about civil, not criminal, judgments; not an absence of national criminal-law enforcement.

5. Trade freedom and permitted restrictions

  • 301: free trade, commerce and intercourse across India, including inter-State and intra-State; aim a common economic space. Regulatory measures and all taxes are not automatically prohibited restrictions.
  • 302: Parliament restricts in public interest. 303: neither level ordinarily gives State preference/discrimination through trade entries; Parliament's scarcity-of-goods exception permitted by 303(2).
  • 304(a): State can tax imported goods if similar local goods bear same treatment; no discrimination against imports from other States/UTs.
  • 304(b): State can impose reasonable public-interest restrictions; introduction/moving amendment requires prior presidential sanction. Distinguish clause (a)'s non-discriminatory tax from clause (b)'s trade restrictions.
  • 305: saves specified existing laws and State-monopoly laws within constitutional conditions. Government trade/business/industry/service may exclude private participation wholly/partly.
  • 307: Parliament may create implementation authority for 301-304; chapter notes none created. Its US Inter-State Commerce Commission comparison is historical, not a statement that that US body still exists.

6. Five Zonal Councils

  • Statutory, advisory/deliberative: States Reorganisation Act, 1956; no judicial enforcement power. Zones reflect geography, rivers/communications, cultural/linguistic affinity, economic development, security and law/order.
  • Union Home Minister chairs all five; CMs act as Vice-Chair by rotation for one year. Members: CMs + two other Ministers from each State, UT administrator as provided. Advisors without vote: nominated planning/policy representative, chief secretaries, development commissioners; NITI-associated participation reflects current institutional practice.
  • Northern - New Delhi: Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Delhi, Chandigarh, J&K, Ladakh. Central - Prayagraj: UP, Uttarakhand, MP, Chhattisgarh.
  • Eastern - Kolkata: Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal. Western - Mumbai: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, merged UT Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.
  • Southern - Chennai: AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry. Newer official meetings also include Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep; textbook lists/older MHA webpages can be incomplete. Headquarters in the chapter are conventional zonal locations; the common Secretariat is in Delhi.
  • Objectives: national/emotional integration; curb divisive regionalism/linguism; smooth reorganisation's after-effects; exchange experience; coordinate social/economic policy and major development projects; balance regional interests.
  • Subjects: economic/social planning, linguistic minorities, borders, inter-State transport and other shared concerns. Boundary issue discussed ≠ council can unilaterally redraw boundaries.

7. North-Eastern Council

  • Separate statutory council: NEC Act 1971, operational 8 August 1972; not a sixth Zonal Council under the 1956 Act.
  • Eight States: Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Sikkim; Sikkim added by 2002 amendment.
  • Regional planning/coordination and review of development; textbook security/public-order description reflects original functions. 2002 amendment made NEC the regional planning body; do not copy superseded functions as its current statutory mandate without qualification.

8. One-minute recall / Mains

  • 262 tribunal; 263 council; 261 recognition; 301 freedom. ISC = constitutional basis/PM; Zonal = 1956 statute/Home Minister; NEC = 1971 separate statute/eight States.
  • 304(a): non-discriminatory tax; 304(b): reasonable restriction + prior presidential sanction. Council advice ≠ binding tribunal/court decision.
  • Mains: dispute/problem → constitutional mechanism → delays/implementation/cooperation challenge → negotiation, reliable data, effective institutions and accountable compliance.

References

  • Official Constitution: Articles 261-263 and Part XIII.
  • MHA annual report: Southern Zonal Council participation.

# Emergency Provisions

## 1. Three constitutional mechanisms

- **Part XVIII, 352-360:** exceptional powers protect security, constitutional government and financial stability. They centralise authority without formally rewriting the federal structure; **constitutional limits and judicial review remain**.
- **352 - National Emergency:** war, external aggression, armed rebellion threatening security of India/part. **356 - President's Rule:** State government cannot function constitutionally. **360 - Financial Emergency:** financial stability/credit of India/part threatened.
- “National Emergency”, “State Emergency” and “constitutional emergency” are common labels; 352 says Proclamation of Emergency, 356 does not itself use “emergency”.

![Three separate grounds and procedures.](Revision%20Diagrams/compare.svg)

*Three separate grounds and procedures.*

## 2. National Emergency: grounds and safeguards

- Actual or **imminent danger** of war/external aggression/armed rebellion suffices. Multiple proclamations on different grounds may coexist (**38th Amendment, 1975**); whole India or specified part (**42nd, 1976**).
- **44th Amendment, 1978:** replaced vague “internal disturbance” by **armed rebellion**; **internal disturbance remains in 355**, but is insufficient by itself for 352.
- **Written Union Cabinet decision is mandatory**: PM alone cannot supply the constitutional recommendation. Cabinet here = PM + Cabinet-rank Ministers, not entire Council of Ministers.
- 38th's attempt to immunise presidential satisfaction from review removed by 44th; mala fides, irrelevant/extraneous grounds and perversity can be reviewed. Chapter links this to **Minerva Mills, 1980**; do not confuse this with that case's main amendment/basic-structure holding.

## 3. Approval, continuation and revocation: 352

- Both Houses approve **within one month**. Each needs **majority of total membership + at least two-thirds present/voting**. After approval, continued for **six months at a time**; no fixed maximum if valid periodic approvals continue.
- Lok Sabha dissolved during initial/further approval period: Rajya Sabha approval plus approval by new Lok Sabha **within 30 days of its first sitting** preserves proclamation. Not a general exemption from Lok Sabha approval.
- President may revoke by later proclamation; **revocation needs no parliamentary approval**. Must revoke if Lok Sabha disapproves continuation by **simple majority**.
- **One-tenth total LS members** give written notice to Speaker (President if House not sitting) → special sitting **within 14 days** to consider disapproval. **Approval = both Houses/special majority; disapproval = LS only/simple majority**.
- 44th shortened initial approval from two months to one, added recurring approval/special majority and parliamentary revocation safeguards.

![Article 352 approval and revocation safeguards.](Revision%20Diagrams/national.svg)

*Article 352 approval and revocation safeguards.*

## 4. Effects on federal relations and legislative terms

- **353 executive:** Union directs States on any executive matter; State governments do not automatically disappear. **250 legislative:** Parliament legislates on State subjects/GST; States still legislate but inconsistent State law yields while Union law operates.
- State-subject laws under 250 cease **six months after Emergency ends**; valid past acts protected as provided. President may issue ordinances when **both Houses are not simultaneously in session** and 123 conditions satisfied; one House's recess can suffice.
- Under a geographically limited Emergency, 353 effects can reach other States **when security of India/part is threatened by activities in or relating to the affected part**; do not state unconditional nationwide extension.
- **354:** President modifies operation of revenue-distribution provisions **268-279**, order laid before both Houses; cannot extend beyond end of financial year when Emergency ceases.
- **83(2)/172(1):** Parliament extends LS/State Assembly term **up to one year at a time**, not beyond **six months after Emergency ends**. Fifth LS extension authorised twice; dissolved **18 January 1977** before second extended end date.

## 5. Article 358 versus Article 359

- **358:** Article **19** restraints relax **automatically**, only during **war/external-aggression** Emergency, **not armed rebellion**. No separate presidential order needed.
- **359:** President's order suspends **right to seek court enforcement** of specified Part III rights and pending proceedings for stated period; **Articles 20 and 21 cannot be included**. Requires order; available for external or armed-rebellion Emergency; whole/part territory, with constitutional conditions.
- **359 order laid before each House as soon as possible**; Article does **not require a separate parliamentary approval vote** merely because it is laid.
- Both 358/359(1A) protections are limited to laws containing the required **Emergency-related recital**, and executive action under such law. Do not assume arbitrary unrelated action becomes immune, or all legal remedies disappear.
- When special protection/order ends, inconsistent law ceases prospectively to that extent; constitutionally protected past action is not retrospectively invalidated merely because rights restraints return.
- **Territorial trap:** textbook says 358 always whole India. Where Emergency confined to part, 358's proviso conditionally permits protected laws/action elsewhere if security threatened by activities in/related to emergency area; **not an unconditional blanket geographic rule**.
- **Recall:** 358 = **19 / automatic / external only**; 359 = **specified enforcement / presidential order / both grounds / never 20-21**.

![Rights and judicial enforcement must be distinguished.](Revision%20Diagrams/rights.svg)

*Rights and judicial enforcement must be distinguished.*

## 6. National Emergency history

- **October 1962-January 1968:** external aggression, China/NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh); continued through **1965 Pakistan war**, so no fresh proclamation then.
- **December 1971-March 1977:** external aggression, Pakistan. **June 1975-March 1977:** internal disturbance, coexisted with 1971 proclamation; old ground no longer available under 352.
- **1975 Emergency:** controversial restrictions/abuse; 1977 election brought Janata government; **Shah Commission** investigated, criticised justification; **44th Amendment** strengthened safeguards.

## 7. President's Rule: grounds and duration

- **355:** Union duty to protect States and ensure constitutional government. **356:** President's satisfaction on **Governor report or otherwise**. **365:** non-compliance with constitutional Union directions may support breakdown finding; not automatic imposition.
- Both Houses approve **within two months**, **simple majority**. Initially lasts **six months from proclamation**, renewed every six months; **ordinary maximum three years**.
- Lok Sabha dissolution rule: RS approval plus LS approval **within 30 days of reconstituted House's first sitting** applies to initial/continuation approval.
- **Beyond one year, both conditions required:** National Emergency operating in whole India or whole/part concerned State **and** EC certification that elections cannot be held owing to difficulties. One condition alone insufficient.
- **Historical Punjab exception:** rule beginning May 1987 continued up to five years through special amendments, including **68th Amendment, 1991**; not today's general maximum.
- President may revoke anytime by proclamation, without parliamentary approval. No equivalent 352 special LS-disapproval procedure in 356.

## 8. President's Rule: what changes and what remains

- President assumes State executive functions/Governor or other executive powers as provided; State ministry dismissed; Governor administers with officials/advisors. Legislature suspended/dissolved; parliamentary legislative/budget authority.
- **357:** Parliament can confer State legislative power on President/other authority; conferral of duties on Union officers; President may authorise State Consolidated Fund spending pending parliamentary sanction when LS not sitting.
- **State laws made during President's Rule survive restoration**, until competent authority alters/repeals/re-enacts. Compare 250 laws' six-month expiry.
- **HC powers/status cannot be assumed or suspended**; President's Rule does **not automatically suspend Fundamental Rights**.
- Under Bommai, Assembly normally kept suspended until parliamentary approval before irreversible dissolution; unconstitutional proclamation can be invalidated and government/Assembly restored.

## 9. Bommai and proper use of 356

- **S.R. Bommai, 1994:** judicial review; relevant material necessary; Union must justify challenged action; court assesses relevance, mala fides/perversity, not ordinary political merits. Restoration possible.
- **Floor test** resolves genuine majority doubts; Governor's personal assessment is insufficient. New Union ruling party cannot remove State ministries merely because opposition governs them. **Federalism and secularism are basic structure**.
- Potentially proper: hung House **after realistic alternatives explored**; majority party refuses and no coalition possible; defeated ministry resigns/no alternative; deliberate constitutional subversion; wilful failure of constitutional duties endangering security; disregard of valid constitutional Union direction that actually warrants breakdown finding.
- Improper: skipping alternatives/floor test; defeat in LS election despite State-Assembly majority; ordinary disturbance short of breakdown; mere maladministration/corruption allegations/financial pressure; partisan/intra-party aims; no warning/opportunity to correct except urgent disastrous situation.
- Historical examples: first **Punjab, 1951**; **nine State dismissals 1977**, repeated against nine in **1980**; **1992 MP/Himachal/Rajasthan** upheld on secularism grounds; Nagaland 1988, Karnataka 1989, Meghalaya 1991 cases were not upheld.
- Ambedkar hoped 356 would remain exceptional/“dead letter”; chapter's **125+ uses** is a dated textbook tally, not an updated count.

## 10. Financial Emergency - Article 360

- Trigger: threatened financial stability/credit of India or any part. Both Houses approve **within two months**, **simple majority**; LS dissolution safeguard = RS approval + **30 days after new LS first sitting**.
- Once approved, **indefinite until revoked; no six-monthly renewal or fixed maximum**. President revokes without parliamentary approval. Satisfaction reviewable after 44th removed 38th immunity.
- Union directs financial propriety and other necessary measures; State salaries/allowances may be reduced; specified Money/financial Bills reserved after passage. Union salaries and **SC/HC judges' salaries/allowances** may also be reduced under directions.
- No automatic suspension of Fundamental Rights. Chapter records **none declared**, even during 1991 crisis; distinguish economic hardship from a formally proclaimed 360 Emergency.
- Ambedkar compared the emergency financial response to US recovery measures during Great Depression; comparison is historical justification, not identical legal machinery.

## 11. Debate and one-minute recall

- Critics: **H.V. Kamath** - danger to liberty/federalism; **K.T. Shah** - strengthening Centre over units and government over people; **T.T. Krishnamachari** - executive dictatorship; **H.N. Kunzru** - loss of State financial autonomy.
- Supporters: **Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar** - constitutional survival; **Mahabir Tyagi** - safety valve; **Ambedkar** - necessity while acknowledging potential political abuse.
- **352: 1 month / special / 6-month renewals / no fixed maximum. 356: 2 months / simple / 6-month renewals / ordinarily 3 years. 360: 2 months / simple / no recurring renewal / no fixed maximum.**
- Mains: exceptional necessity → centralising/rights risks → written Cabinet decision, parliamentary control, protected 20/21, floor test/judicial review → proportional use and constitutional accountability.

## Reference

- [Official Constitution: Part XVIII; approval, territorial provisos and rights safeguards](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/359f70a69695affb9d72f8393102bd2e.pdf).

chapters.markdown:
# President

## 1. Constitutional position and election

- **52-78, Part V:** Union executive comprises President, Vice-President, PM, Council of Ministers and Attorney-General. President = **Head of State/first citizen**, symbol of unity; PM-led ministry exercises real executive authority.
- **54 electoral college:** **elected MPs of both Houses + elected State Assembly members + elected Delhi/Puducherry Assembly members**. UT inclusion follows **70th Amendment, 1992** (effective 1995); do not automatically include every UT Assembly.
- Excluded: nominated MPs/MLAs; **all Legislative Council members**. A dissolved Assembly has no electors until reconstituted; vacancies do not invalidate presidential election.
- **55:** uniform State representation and approximate Union-State parity; indirect election suits parliamentary government, avoids costly direct mandate and preserves State participation. Constitution calls it proportional representation/STV; for **one office**, it functions as preferential transferable voting, not proportional allocation among several seats.
- **Secret ballot; one ballot, ranked preferences; weighted vote values.** No party whip binds presidential voting. Quota = **floor(total valid vote value ÷ 2) + 1**. Count first preferences; if no quota, eliminate lowest candidate, transfer according to next available preferences under counting rules; continue to result.
- **71:** SC decides presidential-election disputes, decision final; incomplete college no ground by itself; acts before election declared void remain valid.

## 2. Vote-value calculation

- **MLA:** State's **1971 population ÷ elected Assembly strength ÷ 1,000**; if remainder after multiples of 1,000 is **at least 500**, add one. Value applies to each elected MLA, not population-proportional ballots cast separately.
- **MP:** total assigned MLA vote value ÷ total elected strength of both parliamentary Houses; fraction **greater than one-half rounds up**, other fractions disregarded.
- **84th Amendment, 2001:** 1971 population continues until figures of **first census taken after 2026** are published; it does not automatically switch population base on 1 January 2027.
- **2022 illustration, not fixed forever:** 4,033 Assembly electors + 776 MPs (543 LS + 233 RS) = **4,809 electors**; each MP value **700**; MLA total **5,43,231**, MP total **5,43,200**, combined **10,86,431**. Actual voters/valid votes may differ from authorised total.
- **2022 MLA values:** AP 159; Arunachal 8; Assam 116; Bihar 173; Chhattisgarh 129; Goa 20; Gujarat 147; Haryana 112; Himachal 51; Jharkhand 176; Karnataka 131; Kerala 152; MP 131; Maharashtra **175**; Manipur 18; Meghalaya 17; Mizoram 8; Nagaland 9; Odisha 149; Punjab 116; Rajasthan 129; Sikkim 7; Tamil Nadu 176; Telangana 132; Tripura 26; Uttarakhand 64; UP **208**; West Bengal 151; Delhi 58; Puducherry 16.
- Table arithmetic correction: Maharashtra **175 × 288 = 50,400**, not 178 × 288. **UP highest MLA value; Sikkim lowest (2022)**. Population/seat figures are inputs to formula, not current demographic statistics.

![Election method and representation.](Revision%20Diagrams/election.svg)

*Election method and representation.*

## 3. Qualifications, nomination and oath

- **58:** Indian citizen, **35+**, qualified for Lok Sabha election, no prohibited office of profit. Sitting President/VP, Governor and Union/State Minister are constitutional exceptions to office-of-profit disqualification.
- **50 proposers + 50 seconders; ₹15,000 deposit**. Before 1997: 10 each/₹2,500. Statutory forfeiture: unsuccessful candidate whose valid votes **do not exceed one-sixth of votes necessary to secure election**; do not substitute the ordinary constituency-election “one-sixth of valid votes polled” formula.
- **60 oath:** faithfully execute office; preserve/protect/defend Constitution and law; serve people's well-being. Administered by **CJI**, or senior-most available SC judge in absence; acting/discharging President also takes oath.
- **59 conditions:** cannot remain MP/State legislator; seat vacated on assuming Presidency; no other office of profit; official residence rent-free; emoluments/allowances fixed by Parliament, **not reduced during term**.
- Salary increased to **₹5 lakh/month** by Finance Act 2018, effective **1 January 2016**. Retired President pension **50% of presidential emoluments/month**; furnished residence, staff, office, medical/travel benefits under law; qualifying deceased President's spouse pension **50% of retired-President pension**. Chapter's ₹1 lakh/₹20,000 annual office-expense figures are historical statutory figures, not salary or pension amounts.
- **361 immunity:** not answerable to courts for official performance; no criminal proceedings/arrest/imprisonment during term; personal civil proceedings require **two months' written notice**. Governmental action remains reviewable; immunity does not prevent impeachment/investigative House procedure.

## 4. Term, impeachment and vacancies

- **56/57:** five years from entry; resign to **Vice-President**; eligible for repeated re-election, **no Indian two-term ceiling**; outgoing President continues until successor assumes office. Rajendra Prasad served two terms.
- **61 impeachment:** “violation of Constitution” (not defined); either House initiates. Notice signed by **at least one-fourth total members**, **14 days' notice**; initiating resolution **at least two-thirds total membership**.
- Other House investigates; President may appear/be represented. If charges sustained by **at least two-thirds total membership**, removal effective that resolution's date. **Not two-thirds merely present/voting**.
- **Nominated MPs participate in impeachment; MLAs do not**. Quasi-judicial parliamentary procedure; distinguish electoral college from investigating/removing body.
- **62:** term-end election before expiry; holdover if delayed, so VP does not automatically take over at five-year mark. Casual vacancy (death/resignation/removal/otherwise): election **within six months**, successor gets **full five-year term**.
- VP acts during casual vacancy or discharges functions during temporary incapacity. If both offices unavailable, **CJI/senior-most available SC judge** under President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969. Acting person receives presidential powers/immunities/emoluments.
- Death in office: **Zakir Husain 1969; Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed 1977**. **V.V. Giri** acted in 1969, then resigned VP to contest; **CJI M. Hidayatullah** discharged functions until new President took office.

*Article 61: use total-membership thresholds.*

## 5. Executive and legislative powers

- **53/77:** Union executive action in President's name; authentication, business-transaction and ministerial allocation rules. PM appointed; other Ministers on PM advice; pleasure exercised consistently with parliamentary responsibility.
- Appointments include Attorney-General, CAG, EC members, UPSC chair/members, Governors, FC chair/members, SC/HC judges **under respective constitutional/statutory procedures**, not unlimited personal choice.
- **78:** seek administration/legislation information from PM; require individual Minister's decision placed before Council. Appoint specified backward-class commission/ISC; UT administration through administrators; Scheduled/tribal-area powers.
- **85/87/88:** summon/prorogue Parliament, dissolve **LS only**; joint sitting called under 108, presided by LS Speaker; special address after each general election and first session each year; messages to Houses.
- If both presiding offices vacant, appoint specified member to perform LS Speaker/RS Chairman duties. **12 nominated RS members:** literature, science, art, social service. Anglo-Indian LS nomination ceased **25 January 2020** under the 104th Amendment changes; not a current two-member nomination power.
- Parliamentary disqualification under **103:** President decides according to EC opinion in applicable cases; **anti-defection decided by House presiding officer**, not all disqualifications by President.
- Prior recommendation: **3** State reorganisation; **Money Bills under 110/117**; financial Bills as specified; **274** State-interested taxes/distribution. Bill involving CFI expenditure may require recommendation **before passage**, not necessarily introduction. **304(b)** specified State trade-restriction Bills need prior sanction.
- Causes CAG/UPSC/FC reports to be laid; regulations for specified UTs, with Puducherry conditions; Ladakh regulatory route under **J&K Reorganisation Act 58(2)**.

## 6. Financial, judicial, diplomatic, military and emergency powers

- **112:** annual financial statement laid; Money Bills require recommendation; no grant demand without recommendation; Contingency Fund advances under law; **FC every five years or earlier**.
- Appoints SC/HC judges; **143** references public-important law/fact questions to SC under its conditions; advice generally advisory, not an appellate judgment between litigants. **72** clemency power.
- Represents State externally; treaties/diplomatic credentials in President's name. **Not every treaty requires prior parliamentary ratification**; legislation may be necessary where domestic law/rights need change, notably under **253**.
- Supreme command of defence forces; service chiefs appointed through government process; war/peace decisions within constitutional parliamentary/executive framework, not unilateral personal military authority.
- **352:** security Emergency, written Cabinet advice; **356/365:** constitutional State breakdown; **360:** financial stability/credit. **359** enforcement order cannot include 20/21; 358 applies only to 19/external Emergency. President's Rule cannot assume HC powers.

- Must be laid before both Houses; ceases **six weeks after reassembly**, calculated from **later date** if Houses reassemble differently; earlier if both pass disapproval (later resolution controls); President may withdraw on advice.
- Continuing legislation requires parliamentary enactment replacing ordinance, **not a resolution magically converting it into an Act**. Chapter's **six months + six weeks** is a conventional maximum illustration using session-gap rule; remember actual constitutional reassembly/expiry rules.

*Ordinances require legislative scrutiny.*

- **K.R. Narayanan:** returned UP President's Rule recommendation **October 1997**, Cabinet withdrew; returned Bihar proposal **September 1998**, later renewed advice led to Rule **February 1999**.

## 11. Presidential election chronology in the chapter

- **1969 V.V. Giri** (50.22%), N. Sanjeeva Reddy. **1974 Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed** (80.18%), Tridib Chaudhuri. **1977 N. Sanjeeva Reddy unopposed**.
- **1982 Giani Zail Singh** (72.73%), H.R. Khanna; **1987 R. Venkataraman** (72.29%), V.R. Krishna Iyer; **1992 Shankar Dayal Sharma** (65.86%), George Swell; **1997 K.R. Narayanan** (94.97%), T.N. Seshan.
- **2002 A.P.J. Abdul Kalam** (89.58%), Lakshmi Sahgal; **2007 Pratibha Patil** (65.82%), B.S. Shekhawat; **2012 Pranab Mukherjee** (**69.31%**, calculated from 7,13,763 of 10,29,750 valid vote value; chapter percentage is incorrect), P.A. Sangma; **2017 Ram Nath Kovind** (65.65%), Meira Kumar; **2022 Droupadi Murmu** (64.03%), Yashwant Sinha. Percentages are historical chapter figures, not vote-share predictions.
- First woman President **Pratibha Patil**; Murmu first tribal woman President. **1977 only unopposed election in chapter; 1969 highly competitive; Rajendra Prasad alone repeated elected full term**.

## 12. One-minute recall

- **President election = elected MPs + elected MLAs; impeachment = all MPs, no MLAs. 35 years; 50+50; ₹15,000; five years; casual election six months.**
- **61 = two-thirds TOTAL in each House; 352 approval = total majority + two-thirds PRESENT/VOTING.**
- **111 repassed Union ordinary Bill binds; 201 repassed reserved State Bill does not. 123 = later reassembly + six weeks. 72 = Union / military / death.**
- Head of State exercises constitutional power **through responsible government**, with limited safeguards, consultation and situational judgment.

## References

- [Constitution](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/359f70a69695affb9d72f8393102bd2e.pdf) · [ECI election rules](https://www.eci.gov.in/faq/1/2) · [Emoluments Act](https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2107/1/A1951-30.pdf).
- [SC assent opinion, 2025](https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2025/39157/39157_2025_1_1501_66169_Judgement_20-Nov-2025.pdf) · [SC ordinance-survival discussion](https://webapi.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2019/29796/29796_2019_1_1501_49019_Judgement_11-Dec-2023.pdf).

chapters.markdown:
# Vice-President

## 1. Office and electoral college

- **63:** Vice-President; second-highest constitutional office/warrant-of-precedence rank after President; institutional continuity. US office supplied comparison, but succession rules differ.
- **66:** electoral college = **all MPs of both Houses, elected AND nominated**; **no MLAs/MLCs**. No joint meeting required since **11th Amendment, 1961**.
- Secret ballot, constitutional **proportional representation by single transferable vote**; ranked preferences for one office. **Each MP's vote value is one**; no President-style MLA/MP weighting. Quota = **floor(valid votes ÷ 2) + 1**; transfer preferences when needed.
- **71:** SC decides election disputes finally; incomplete college alone no invalidity; acts before void-election declaration remain valid.
- Reason States excluded: ordinary function is presiding over Rajya Sabha; temporary presidential duty exceptional. President, as Union/State head, has elected Assembly participation.

![Electoral colleges and removal thresholds differ.](Revision%20Diagrams/contrast.svg)

*Electoral colleges and removal thresholds differ.*

## 2. Eligibility, nomination and oath

- Indian citizen; **35+**; qualified for **Rajya Sabha election** (President: LS); no prohibited office of profit. Sitting President/VP, Governor, Union/State Minister exempted for eligibility.
- **20 proposers + 20 seconders; ₹15,000 deposit**. Presidential rule is **50+50**, not interchangeable. Statutory forfeiture for unsuccessful candidate at **not more than one-sixth of votes necessary for election**, not ordinary constituency rule.
- **69 oath:** true faith/allegiance to Constitution; faithfully discharge office. **President or appointed person administers**, not necessarily CJI. Presidential oath separately stresses preserve/protect/defend Constitution.
- Cannot remain member of Parliament/State legislature; seat vacated on entry; no other office of profit. **Ex-officio RS Chairman is not an RS member**.

## 3. Term, resignation and removal

- **67:** five years from entry; may be re-elected repeatedly; holdover until successor enters; resign to **President** (President resigns to VP).
- Removal initiated **only in Rajya Sabha** after **at least 14 days' notice**. RS passes by **majority of all then members** (effective majority: total minus vacancies); LS agrees by **simple majority**.
- **No impeachment**, no specified constitutional removal ground; distinguish President's **two-thirds total membership in both Houses** procedure.
- During own-removal-resolution consideration, VP does not preside; may speak/participate under **92**, but cannot vote on that resolution or any other matter in those proceedings. Normally Chairman only exercises **casting vote on equality**, not ordinary first-instance vote.

![Article 67: only Rajya Sabha initiates.](Revision%20Diagrams/removal.svg)

*Article 67: only Rajya Sabha initiates.*

## 4. Vacancy and presidential duty

- Term-end election before expiry. Casual vacancy (death/resignation/removal/disqualification/void election): election **as soon as possible**, **no constitutionally specified six-month VP-vacancy deadline**. Successor gets **full five years**.
- **65:** during casual presidential vacancy, VP acts until new President enters; presidential election due **within six months**. For temporary presidential incapacity, discharges functions until President resumes; do not apply six months as blanket limit to every incapacity case.
- While acting/discharging President, **does not chair RS**; Deputy Chairman performs duties (other constitutional arrangements if unavailable). Receives presidential powers/immunities/emoluments, **not both salaries**.
- **70:** Parliament provides other presidential-function contingencies; if both offices unavailable, CJI/senior-most available SC judge under 1969 Act.
- **India:** acting President temporarily; **USA:** VP succeeds to Presidency for remainder of predecessor's term. No automatic Indian succession for unexpired term.

## 5. Emoluments and historical examples

- No separate VP-capacity salary: remuneration as **RS Chairman**. Finance Act 2018 raised it to **₹4 lakh/month**, effective **1 January 2016**; pension under law **50% of corresponding emoluments**, with residence/medical/travel benefits. Acting President receives presidential remuneration instead.
- **V.V. Giri acted after Zakir Husain's death (1969); B.D. Jatti after Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed's death (1977)**. Radhakrishnan discharged functions during Rajendra Prasad's **1960 USSR visit/1961 illness**.
- **Krishna Kant:** first VP to die in office (2002). **Radhakrishnan and Hamid Ansari** each elected twice. Nickname “His Superfluous Highness” reflects commentary about limited independent executive functions, not constitutional designation.

## 6. Election chronology

- **1952/1957 S. Radhakrishnan - unopposed**; **1962 Zakir Husain** (568; rival N. Samant Singh 14); **1967 V.V. Giri** (486; Prof. Habib 192).
- **1969 G.S. Pathak** (400; H.V. Kamath 156); **1974 B.D. Jatti** (521; N.E. Horo 141); **1979 M. Hidayatullah - unopposed**.
