Vice-President

1. Office and electoral college

  • 63: Vice-President; second-highest constitutional office/warrant-of-precedence rank after President; institutional continuity. US office supplied comparison, but succession rules differ.
  • 66: electoral college = all MPs of both Houses, elected AND nominated; no MLAs/MLCs. No joint meeting required since 11th Amendment, 1961.
  • Secret ballot, constitutional proportional representation by single transferable vote; ranked preferences for one office. Each MP's vote value is one; no President-style MLA/MP weighting. Quota = floor(valid votes ÷ 2) + 1; transfer preferences when needed.
  • 71: SC decides election disputes finally; incomplete college alone no invalidity; acts before void-election declaration remain valid.
  • Reason States excluded: ordinary function is presiding over Rajya Sabha; temporary presidential duty exceptional. President, as Union/State head, has elected Assembly participation.

2. Eligibility, nomination and oath

  • Indian citizen; 35+; qualified for Rajya Sabha election (President: LS); no prohibited office of profit. Sitting President/VP, Governor, Union/State Minister exempted for eligibility.
  • 20 proposers + 20 seconders; ₹15,000 deposit. Presidential rule is 50+50, not interchangeable. Statutory forfeiture for unsuccessful candidate at not more than one-sixth of votes necessary for election, not ordinary constituency rule.
  • 69 oath: true faith/allegiance to Constitution; faithfully discharge office. President or appointed person administers, not necessarily CJI. Presidential oath separately stresses preserve/protect/defend Constitution.
  • Cannot remain member of Parliament/State legislature; seat vacated on entry; no other office of profit. Ex-officio RS Chairman is not an RS member.

3. Term, resignation and removal

  • 67: five years from entry; may be re-elected repeatedly; holdover until successor enters; resign to President (President resigns to VP).
  • Removal initiated only in Rajya Sabha after at least 14 days' notice. RS passes by majority of all then members (effective majority: total minus vacancies); LS agrees by simple majority.
  • No impeachment, no specified constitutional removal ground; distinguish President's two-thirds total membership in both Houses procedure.
  • During own-removal-resolution consideration, VP does not preside; may speak/participate under 92, but cannot vote on that resolution or any other matter in those proceedings. Normally Chairman only exercises casting vote on equality, not ordinary first-instance vote.

4. Vacancy and presidential duty

  • Term-end election before expiry. Casual vacancy (death/resignation/removal/disqualification/void election): election as soon as possible, no constitutionally specified six-month VP-vacancy deadline. Successor gets full five years.
  • 65: during casual presidential vacancy, VP acts until new President enters; presidential election due within six months. For temporary presidential incapacity, discharges functions until President resumes; do not apply six months as blanket limit to every incapacity case.
  • While acting/discharging President, does not chair RS; Deputy Chairman performs duties (other constitutional arrangements if unavailable). Receives presidential powers/immunities/emoluments, not both salaries.
  • 70: Parliament provides other presidential-function contingencies; if both offices unavailable, CJI/senior-most available SC judge under 1969 Act.
  • India: acting President temporarily; USA: VP succeeds to Presidency for remainder of predecessor's term. No automatic Indian succession for unexpired term.

5. Emoluments and historical examples

  • No separate VP-capacity salary: remuneration as RS Chairman. Finance Act 2018 raised it to ₹4 lakh/month, effective 1 January 2016; pension under law 50% of corresponding emoluments, with residence/medical/travel benefits. Acting President receives presidential remuneration instead.
  • V.V. Giri acted after Zakir Husain's death (1969); B.D. Jatti after Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed's death (1977). Radhakrishnan discharged functions during Rajendra Prasad's 1960 USSR visit/1961 illness.
  • Krishna Kant: first VP to die in office (2002). Radhakrishnan and Hamid Ansari each elected twice. Nickname “His Superfluous Highness” reflects commentary about limited independent executive functions, not constitutional designation.

6. Election chronology

  • 1952/1957 S. Radhakrishnan - unopposed; 1962 Zakir Husain (568; rival N. Samant Singh 14); 1967 V.V. Giri (486; Prof. Habib 192).
  • 1969 G.S. Pathak (400; H.V. Kamath 156); 1974 B.D. Jatti (521; N.E. Horo 141); 1979 M. Hidayatullah - unopposed.
  • 1984 R. Venkataraman (508; B.C. Kamble 207); 1987 Shankar Dayal Sharma - unopposed; 1992 K.R. Narayanan (700; Kaka Joginder Singh 1).
  • 1997 Krishna Kant (441; Surjit Singh Barnala 273); 2002 B.S. Shekhawat (454; Sushil Kumar Shinde 305); 2007 Hamid Ansari (455; Najma Heptulla 222); 2012 Ansari (490; Jaswant Singh 238).
  • 2017 M. Venkaiah Naidu (516; Gopal Krishna Gandhi 244); 2022 Jagdeep Dhankhar (528; Margaret Alva 182). These are chapter's historical election results.
  • 2025 update: C.P. Radhakrishnan elected, 452 vs B. Sudershan Reddy 300, sworn 12 September 2025; 15th person to hold office because repeated elections are not new office-holders. Official announcement · Akashvani result.

7. One-minute recall

  • All MPs / no MLAs / equal vote; 35 years / RS eligibility / 20+20 / ₹15,000. Five years; resign to President.
  • Removal: RS effective + LS simple + 14-day notice; no impeachment. VP vacancy ASAP; presidential vacancy election six months.
  • RS Chairman ≠ RS member; no chairing RS while acting as President; India acting succession ≠ US permanent succession.

  • ECI: VP election procedure.

# Prime Minister

## 1. Appointment and parliamentary confidence

- **President = Head of State/formal executive; PM = Head of Government/real executive leader**, operating through the Council of Ministers.
- **75:** President appoints PM; Constitution prescribes no popular/direct PM election or detailed party-selection procedure. With clear LS majority, appoint its leader; with hung House, select person **likely to command confidence**, coalition/support evidence matters.
- Largest party alone has no absolute constitutional entitlement. Floor test within **reasonable time**, not an invariable constitutional “one-month” limit. Appointment need not await a prior confidence vote; majority must subsequently be established when required.
- **1979:** N. Sanjeeva Reddy appointed Charan Singh after Morarji Desai government's fall. Examples of appointment before proving confidence: Charan Singh 1979; V.P. Singh 1989; Chandra Shekhar 1990; P.V. Narasimha Rao 1991; Vajpayee 1996/1998; Deve Gowda 1996; Gujral 1997.
- Sudden death/no clear successor requires situational presidential judgment: **1964/1966 Gulzarilal Nanda interim PM** after Nehru/Shastri; **1984 Rajiv Gandhi** appointed after Indira's assassination, then confirmed as party leader.
- **75(5):** non-MP may be appointed but must enter **either House within six consecutive months**, otherwise ceases to be Minister/PM; no recurring appointments to evade rule. SC upheld non-MP PM appointment in **1996**.
- PM may belong to **LS or RS**: Indira Gandhi at initial 1966 appointment, Deve Gowda after 1996 parliamentary entry, Manmohan Singh 2004 were RS-associated examples. **Deve Gowda initially not an MP**, so do not imply he was already RS member at appointment.

![Appointment depends on parliamentary confidence.](Revision%20Diagrams/appointment.svg)

*Appointment depends on parliamentary confidence.*

## 2. Oath, tenure and emoluments

- President administers **office and secrecy oaths** under **75(4)/Third Schedule**: constitutional allegiance; sovereignty/integrity; faithful conscientious duty; justice without fear/favour, affection/ill-will; confidentiality except due official discharge.
- **No fixed PM term**; presidential pleasure operates through **LS confidence**, not arbitrary dismissal of a majority-backed government. Loss of confidence → resignation or constitutional replacement after majority determination.
- Pay/allowances governed by Parliament, including Ministers' Salaries/Allowances Act, 1952: MP-linked remuneration plus prescribed sumptuary/residence/travel/medical facilities. Chapter records PM sumptuary allowance rise **₹1,500 → ₹3,000/month in 2001**; not total salary.

## 3. PM and Council of Ministers

- Recommends persons for presidential ministerial appointment; allocates/reshuffles portfolios; asks Minister to resign or recommends removal; chairs Cabinet/Council discussions and coordinates policy.
- Guides, directs and coordinates Ministers; government's cohesion and collective responsibility centre on PM leadership.
- PM resignation/death ends existing ministry's political basis, requiring successor/reconstituted arrangements; **does not imply that public administration stops or no caretaker continuity is possible**. Other Minister's departure usually creates only individual vacancy.
- **Laski's recall:** PM central to ministry's **formation, life and end**.

## 4. PM and President: 74, 75, 78

- **74:** Council aids/advises President; President may ask reconsideration once, must act on reconsidered advice. **75:** PM appointed by President, other Ministers on PM advice; ministry collectively responsible to **LS**.
- **78's three duties:** communicate Council's administration/legislation decisions; supply information President requests; submit individual Minister's decision to Council when President requires.
- PM principal channel of President-ministry communication; advice on appointments operates through **office-specific constitutional/statutory selection processes**, not unilateral selection of every constitutional officer.

![PM connects responsible ministry and President.](Revision%20Diagrams/communication.svg)

*PM connects responsible ministry and President.*

## 5. Parliament and broader leadership

- Advises parliamentary summoning/prorogation; may recommend **LS dissolution**, subject to constitutional consideration where majority lost/alternative exists; announces government policy and manages legislative programme.
- **PM may be RS member**, so textbook “always leader of Lower House” is too broad; government's LS Leader can be another Minister. **88:** Minister can speak/take part in either House and specified committees, but votes only in House of membership.
- Chairs **NITI Aayog**, Inter-State Council, National Integration Council and specified national coordination bodies; chapter also lists National Water Resources Council. These roles arise under respective arrangements, not one omnibus constitutional Article.
- Shapes foreign policy, spokesperson of Union government, political crisis coordination, party/coalition leadership; receives State/public representations; political head of administrative machinery while constitutional/statutory safeguards remain.

## 6. Role descriptions: match person to phrase

- **Lord Morley:** first among equals (**primus inter pares**), keystone of Cabinet arch. **Herbert Morrison:** “first among equals” understates modern authority.
- **William Vernon Harcourt:** moon among lesser stars. **Ivor Jennings:** sun around which planets revolve; all constitutional roads lead to PM.
- **H.J. Laski:** pivot; central to ministry's formation/life/death. **H.R.G. Greaves:** leader masters governmental machinery.
- **W.B. Munro:** captain of State's ship. **Ramsay Muir:** steersman. **R.H. Crossman:** shift from Cabinet to Prime-Ministerial government. **Humphry Berkeley:** criticism of excessive PM power weakening effective parliamentary sovereignty.
- Treat metaphors as commentary: strength varies with majority, party organisation, coalition, Cabinet colleagues, institutions and political circumstances. **Ambedkar:** Indian executive leadership comparable to US President lies chiefly with PM rather than ceremonial President; systems remain different.

## 7. Former Chief Ministers who became PMs

- **Morarji Desai:** Bombay CM **1952-56**, PM **1977**, first non-Congress PM. **Charan Singh:** UP CM **1967-68/1970**, PM **1979**.
- **V.P. Singh:** UP CM, PM **December 1989-November 1990**. **P.V. Narasimha Rao:** AP CM **1971-73**, PM **1991-96**, first PM from South India.
- **H.D. Deve Gowda:** Karnataka CM before PM **June 1996**. **Narendra Modi:** Gujarat CM **2001-14**, PM first took office **May 2014**. Six people in chapter's list; these are historical office transitions.

## 8. Caretaker government: convention and continuity

- Constitution has **no separate caretaker-government category**; responsible ministry continues as necessary after resignation/LS dissolution until new arrangements. Free/fair elections conducted by **ECI**, with administration required to support lawful, neutral process.
- Routine administration and urgent national/security-interest decisions continue; convention discourages **major new policy, avoidable spending, appointments or electoral advantage** without proper justification. Caretaker does not mean all legal executive powers vanish.
- **Tarkunde/JP Committee:** unofficial electoral-reform committee **1974**, report **1975**, chair Justice V.M. Tarkunde; proposed no new policies/projects, allowances/loans/pay rises or partisan minister-attended official functions.
- **August 1979 presidential communique:** government promised neutral elections, no major new policy/spending; urgent national-interest work not held up. Historical proposed Nov-Dec timetable must not be confused with actual later election dates.
- **Calcutta HC, December 1979:** extraordinary continuity arrangement for necessary day-to-day administration until alternative ministry. Restraint rationale: dissolved LS weakens normal parliamentary accountability; outgoing government must not exploit office in elections.
- Distinguish **caretaker convention**, EC's **Model Code of Conduct**, and binding constitutional/statutory duties; they overlap but are not identical.

## 9. One-minute recall / Mains

- **74 advice; 75 appointment/LS responsibility/6 months; 77 government business; 78 communication; 88 participation.**
- **Either House eligible; no fixed term; majority support central; President appoints but does not have unrestricted policy choice.**
- Mains: PM links President-Cabinet-Parliament; leadership enables coordination, while collective responsibility, opposition, courts, federal institutions and internal Cabinet/coalition consultation curb concentration.

## Reference

- [Official Constitution: Articles 74-78 and 88](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/359f70a69695affb9d72f8393102bd2e.pdf).

chapters.markdown:
# Central Council of Ministers

## 1. The parliamentary executive

- **President = constitutional head; Prime Minister-led Council = real political executive.** Council membership is wider than the Cabinet; the Cabinet is its principal decision-making core.
- **Article 74:** Council headed by PM aids/advises President. **42nd Amendment (1976)** made advice binding; **44th Amendment (1978)** allows one reconsideration, after which the reconsidered advice binds.
- **74(2):** courts cannot inquire into whether/what ministerial advice was tendered. This does **not** make underlying material or executive action automatically immune from judicial review.
- **U.N.R. Rao (1971):** Council must continue even when Lok Sabha is dissolved. **Shamsher Singh (1974):** President/Governor normally act on ministerial advice; their constitutional satisfaction ordinarily means ministerial satisfaction.

## 2. Appointment, size and tenure

- **Article 75:** President appoints PM; appoints other ministers **on PM’s advice**. President’s pleasure operates through responsible government: PM can seek a minister’s resignation or advise removal.
- **91st Amendment (2003), 75(1A):** ministers **including PM ≤15% of total Lok Sabha membership**. No constitutional Union minimum of 12; that minimum concerns State ministries.
- **75(1B):** a member disqualified for defection cannot become minister until their original term expires, or—if they contest an election earlier—until declared elected, whichever is earlier. Six-month membership provision cannot bypass disqualification.
- A minister can belong to **either House**. A non-MP may be appointed but must become a member of either House within **six consecutive months**, otherwise ceases to be minister.
- **Article 88:** minister may speak/participate in either House, joint sittings and a parliamentary committee of which nominated a member; this right itself confers no vote. **Votes only in the House of which they are a member.**
- President administers **oaths of office and secrecy**. Office oath: Constitution/allegiance; sovereignty/integrity; faithful duties; justice without fear/favour, affection/ill-will. Secrecy permits disclosure only as necessary for due discharge of duties.
- Parliament determines salaries/allowances by law. **Chapter’s 2001 monthly sumptuary allowance:** PM ₹3,000; Cabinet minister ₹2,000; MoS ₹1,000; deputy minister ₹600 (earlier ₹1,500/1,000/500/300). These are historical allowance figures, **not total current salary**.
- **Deputy PM is a political designation**, with no separate constitutional powers or automatic succession. The Devi Lal oath controversy (1990) did not invalidate his substantive ministerial oath merely because of this designation.

## 3. Responsibility: the key distinction

![Three meanings of ministerial responsibility.](Revision%20Diagrams/responsibility.svg)

*Three meanings of ministerial responsibility.*

- **Collective — 75(3):** entire Council is responsible to **Lok Sabha**, including its Rajya Sabha ministers. All defend agreed government policy; a dissenting minister must resign if unable to support it.
- Lok Sabha’s no-confidence vote brings down the **whole Council**. PM’s resignation also ends the ministry. A defeated Council may advise dissolution; acceptance is not automatic in every situation.
- Historical resignations: **B.R. Ambedkar, 1951**, Hindu Code Bill differences (**1953 in chapter is incorrect**); **C.D. Deshmukh, 1956**, Bombay reorganisation; **Arif Mohammed Khan, 1986**, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) legislation.
- **Individual — 75(2):** a particular minister may be removed on PM’s advice even when the ministry retains Lok Sabha confidence.
- **Legal responsibility:** India has no British-style constitutional requirement that every presidential act be countersigned by a minister who thereby assumes legal responsibility. This **does not exempt ministers from ordinary criminal, civil or statutory liability**.

## 4. Government business and PM’s duties

- **Article 77:** executive action expressed in President’s name; authenticated as prescribed. Proper authentication prevents challenge solely on the ground that President did not personally make the order; other legal defects remain reviewable.
- President makes rules for convenient transaction of government business and allocation among ministers. These rules structure departmental work and Cabinet coordination.
- **Article 78, PM → President:** communicate Council’s administrative/legislative decisions; furnish information sought; place an individual minister’s decision before the Council if President requires it.

## 5. Ranks within the Council

![Cabinet membership differs from departmental charge.](Revision%20Diagrams/ranks.svg)

*Cabinet membership differs from departmental charge.*

- **Cabinet ministers:** major departments/portfolios; Cabinet members; shape government policy and coordinate its implementation.
- **Ministers of State:** either **independent charge** of a ministry/department or **attached** to a Cabinet minister. Independent charge gives departmental responsibility; it does **not** confer Cabinet membership. May attend Cabinet when invited for relevant business.
- **Deputy ministers:** historical junior rank assisting Cabinet ministers/MoS; no independent charge or Cabinet membership. All these ranks need not be present in every ministry.
- **Parliamentary secretaries:** historically appointed to assist ministers in parliamentary work; distinct from constitutionally appointed ministers. Do not treat them as a mandatory present-day Union rank or a way around constitutional size/disqualification rules.

## 6. Council versus Cabinet

- **Council:** all ministers, constitutionally required under 74–75; broader membership; collectively responsible to Lok Sabha; implements government decisions through departments. The claim that it “never meets” is too absolute.
- **Cabinet:** smaller inner body of Cabinet-rank ministers with PM; conducts principal policy deliberation, coordinates departments, gives political direction and handles major decisions. Meeting frequency is practice, **not a constitutional weekly requirement**.
- **Cabinet explicitly defined in 352(3):** PM + other ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under 75; definition inserted by **44th Amendment, 1978**. National Emergency requires its decision communicated **in writing** to President.
- Cabinet leads policymaking, crisis management, legislation, budget priorities, key appointments and foreign policy, subject to law and constitutional procedures. Its influence is extensive; courts, Parliament, rights and federal limits still apply.

## 7. Familiar descriptions of Cabinet power

- **Ramsay Muir:** steering wheel; **Lowell:** keystone of political arch; **Sir John Marriott:** pivot around which political machinery revolves; **Gladstone:** solar orb; **Barker:** magnet of policy.
- **Bagehot:** “hyphen” / “buckle” joining legislature and executive; **Ivor Jennings:** core and source of unity; **L.S. Amery:** central directing instrument of government.
- **“Cabinet dictatorship”** describes strong majority-backed executive dominance; it is a political criticism, not a constitutional grant of unlimited authority.

## 8. Kitchen Cabinet / inner Cabinet

- Informal circle of PM’s trusted advisers: selected ministers and sometimes non-minister associates. Composition varies; **not a constitutional body or necessarily present under every PM**. Indira Gandhi’s era is a prominent chapter example.
- **Benefits:** small group, quick consultation, frequent contact and confidentiality. **Risks:** sidelining formal Cabinet, weak accountability of outsiders and bypassing established procedures.
- Advice from an informal circle does not itself authorise governmental decisions. Formal responsibility, lawful procedure and safeguards for confidential information remain necessary.

## 9. One-minute recall

- **74 = advice; 75 = appointment/size/responsibility; 77 = business; 78 = PM–President information; 88 = participation.**
- **15% includes PM; six months for non-MP; collective responsibility to LS; Cabinet ≠ whole Council; independent-charge MoS ≠ Cabinet member.**
- **Deputy PM ≠ constitutional succession; kitchen Cabinet ≠ formal Cabinet; 352(3) = written Cabinet decision for National Emergency.**

## References

- [Official Constitution](https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/359f70a69695affb9d72f8393102bd2e.pdf) · [PIB: Ambedkar’s resignation in 1951](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/printrelease.aspx?lang=2&reg=48&relid=109313).

1. The parliamentary executive

  • President = constitutional head; Prime Minister-led Council = real political executive. Council membership is wider than the Cabinet; the Cabinet is its principal decision-making core.
  • Article 74: Council headed by PM aids/advises President. 42nd Amendment (1976) made advice binding; 44th Amendment (1978) allows one reconsideration, after which the reconsidered advice binds.
  • 74(2): courts cannot inquire into whether/what ministerial advice was tendered. This does not make underlying material or executive action automatically immune from judicial review.
  • U.N.R. Rao (1971): Council must continue even when Lok Sabha is dissolved. Shamsher Singh (1974): President/Governor normally act on ministerial advice; their constitutional satisfaction ordinarily means ministerial satisfaction.

2. Appointment, size and tenure

  • Article 75: President appoints PM; appoints other ministers on PM’s advice. President’s pleasure operates through responsible government: PM can seek a minister’s resignation or advise removal.
  • 91st Amendment (2003), 75(1A): ministers including PM ≤15% of total Lok Sabha membership. No constitutional Union minimum of 12; that minimum concerns State ministries.
  • 75(1B): a member disqualified for defection cannot become minister until their original term expires, or—if they contest an election earlier—until declared elected, whichever is earlier. Six-month membership provision cannot bypass disqualification.
  • A minister can belong to either House. A non-MP may be appointed but must become a member of either House within six consecutive months, otherwise ceases to be minister.
  • Article 88: minister may speak/participate in either House, joint sittings and a parliamentary committee of which nominated a member; this right itself confers no vote. Votes only in the House of which they are a member.
  • President administers oaths of office and secrecy. Office oath: Constitution/allegiance; sovereignty/integrity; faithful duties; justice without fear/favour, affection/ill-will. Secrecy permits disclosure only as necessary for due discharge of duties.
  • Parliament determines salaries/allowances by law. Chapter’s 2001 monthly sumptuary allowance: PM ₹3,000; Cabinet minister ₹2,000; MoS ₹1,000; deputy minister ₹600 (earlier ₹1,500/1,000/500/300). These are historical allowance figures, not total current salary.
  • Deputy PM is a political designation, with no separate constitutional powers or automatic succession. The Devi Lal oath controversy (1990) did not invalidate his substantive ministerial oath merely because of this designation.

3. Responsibility: the key distinction

  • Collective — 75(3): entire Council is responsible to Lok Sabha, including its Rajya Sabha ministers. All defend agreed government policy; a dissenting minister must resign if unable to support it.
  • Lok Sabha’s no-confidence vote brings down the whole Council. PM’s resignation also ends the ministry. A defeated Council may advise dissolution; acceptance is not automatic in every situation.
  • Historical resignations: B.R. Ambedkar, 1951, Hindu Code Bill differences (1953 in chapter is incorrect); C.D. Deshmukh, 1956, Bombay reorganisation; Arif Mohammed Khan, 1986, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) legislation.
  • Individual — 75(2): a particular minister may be removed on PM’s advice even when the ministry retains Lok Sabha confidence.
  • Legal responsibility: India has no British-style constitutional requirement that every presidential act be countersigned by a minister who thereby assumes legal responsibility. This does not exempt ministers from ordinary criminal, civil or statutory liability.

4. Government business and PM’s duties

  • Article 77: executive action expressed in President’s name; authenticated as prescribed. Proper authentication prevents challenge solely on the ground that President did not personally make the order; other legal defects remain reviewable.
  • President makes rules for convenient transaction of government business and allocation among ministers. These rules structure departmental work and Cabinet coordination.
  • Article 78, PM → President: communicate Council’s administrative/legislative decisions; furnish information sought; place an individual minister’s decision before the Council if President requires it.

5. Ranks within the Council

  • Cabinet ministers: major departments/portfolios; Cabinet members; shape government policy and coordinate its implementation.
  • Ministers of State: either independent charge of a ministry/department or attached to a Cabinet minister. Independent charge gives departmental responsibility; it does not confer Cabinet membership. May attend Cabinet when invited for relevant business.
  • Deputy ministers: historical junior rank assisting Cabinet ministers/MoS; no independent charge or Cabinet membership. All these ranks need not be present in every ministry.
  • Parliamentary secretaries: historically appointed to assist ministers in parliamentary work; distinct from constitutionally appointed ministers. Do not treat them as a mandatory present-day Union rank or a way around constitutional size/disqualification rules.

6. Council versus Cabinet

  • Council: all ministers, constitutionally required under 74–75; broader membership; collectively responsible to Lok Sabha; implements government decisions through departments. The claim that it “never meets” is too absolute.
  • Cabinet: smaller inner body of Cabinet-rank ministers with PM; conducts principal policy deliberation, coordinates departments, gives political direction and handles major decisions. Meeting frequency is practice, not a constitutional weekly requirement.
  • Cabinet explicitly defined in 352(3): PM + other ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under 75; definition inserted by 44th Amendment, 1978. National Emergency requires its decision communicated in writing to President.
  • Cabinet leads policymaking, crisis management, legislation, budget priorities, key appointments and foreign policy, subject to law and constitutional procedures. Its influence is extensive; courts, Parliament, rights and federal limits still apply.

7. Familiar descriptions of Cabinet power

  • Ramsay Muir: steering wheel; Lowell: keystone of political arch; Sir John Marriott: pivot around which political machinery revolves; Gladstone: solar orb; Barker: magnet of policy.
  • Bagehot: “hyphen” / “buckle” joining legislature and executive; Ivor Jennings: core and source of unity; L.S. Amery: central directing instrument of government.
  • “Cabinet dictatorship” describes strong majority-backed executive dominance; it is a political criticism, not a constitutional grant of unlimited authority.

8. Kitchen Cabinet / inner Cabinet

  • Informal circle of PM’s trusted advisers: selected ministers and sometimes non-minister associates. Composition varies; not a constitutional body or necessarily present under every PM. Indira Gandhi’s era is a prominent chapter example.
  • Benefits: small group, quick consultation, frequent contact and confidentiality. Risks: sidelining formal Cabinet, weak accountability of outsiders and bypassing established procedures.
  • Advice from an informal circle does not itself authorise governmental decisions. Formal responsibility, lawful procedure and safeguards for confidential information remain necessary.

9. One-minute recall

  • 74 = advice; 75 = appointment/size/responsibility; 77 = business; 78 = PM–President information; 88 = participation.
  • 15% includes PM; six months for non-MP; collective responsibility to LS; Cabinet ≠ whole Council; independent-charge MoS ≠ Cabinet member.
  • Deputy PM ≠ constitutional succession; kitchen Cabinet ≠ formal Cabinet; 352(3) = written Cabinet decision for National Emergency.

References

  • Official Constitution · PIB: Ambedkar’s resignation in 1951.

# Cabinet Committees

## 1. Why Cabinet uses committees

- **Division of labour + delegation:** reduce Cabinet’s workload; examine specialised issues closely; coordinate ministries; formulate proposals and take authorised decisions.
- **Extra-constitutional:** not named in the Constitution. They operate under the **Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961**, made under **Article 77(3)**; extra-constitutional does not mean unlawful.
- **Standing committees:** continuing bodies, but composition/functions can change. **Ad hoc committees:** temporary, task-specific; dissolved when their work ends. Historical example: **Emergency Committee during the 1962 Chinese invasion**.
- PM determines standing committees’ number, functions and ministerial composition. Ad hoc committees/GoMs may be constituted by **Cabinet, a standing committee or PM**, under Rule 6.
- Usually Cabinet ministers; non-Cabinet ministers may be members or special invitees. Membership includes relevant portfolio ministers and other senior ministers; committee size varies.
- PM chairs committees of which PM is a member; others may be led by senior ministers. **Not every Cabinet Committee is PM-headed.**

![Delegation reduces workload while retaining Cabinet oversight.](Revision%20Diagrams/workflow.svg)

*Delegation reduces workload while retaining Cabinet oversight.*

- Under **Rule 6**, committees can make authorised decisions as well as recommendations; not every case must subsequently go to full Cabinet. Matters reserved for Cabinet and limits on delegation still apply.
- **Cabinet may review committee decisions.** Interdepartmental matters require consultation with concerned departments; committees facilitate coordination rather than replacing it.

## 2. Eight committees: functions to remember

- **Political Affairs:** major domestic/foreign policy matters; intergovernmental political issues. Described in the chapter as **“Super-Cabinet”** because of its wide political influence; this is not a legal superiority over Cabinet.
- **Economic Affairs:** directs/co-ordinates economic policy and governmental economic activity; major economic proposals within its assigned remit.
- **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC):** specified senior appointments/empanelments, including designated central administration, public enterprise, bank and financial-institution posts. It does **not** appoint every government employee or replace constitutional appointment procedures.
- **Parliamentary Affairs:** government’s parliamentary business, priorities and progress.
- **Security:** defence, internal/external security, law-and-order policy issues within Union remit and atomic-energy/security matters. It does not erase State policing powers.
- **Accommodation:** policy/allotment of government accommodation for MPs, central employees and other eligible persons/organisations.
- **Investment and Growth:** investment, capital inflows, growth, exports, import substitution and ease of doing business.
- **Employment and Skill Development** (chapter name): skills, employability and workforce participation, including women. Current name: **Skill, Employment and Livelihood**.

## 3. Official composition update — 27 July 2026

- Official Cabinet Secretariat list retains **eight committees**. It uses **Cabinet Committee on Skill, Employment and Livelihood**, replacing the chapter’s older name. [Official composition](https://cabsec.gov.in/writereaddata/cabinetcommittees/english/1_Upload_4263.pdf).
- **PM leads six:** Appointments, Economic Affairs, Political Affairs, Security, Investment and Growth, Skill/Employment/Livelihood.
- **Accommodation:** Amit Shah heads it. **Parliamentary Affairs:** Raj Nath Singh heads it. Chairmanship and membership are changeable, not constitutionally fixed.
- **ACC:** PM + Amit Shah. **Security:** PM + Defence (Raj Nath Singh), Home (Amit Shah), Finance (Nirmala Sitharaman), External Affairs (S. Jaishankar).
- MoS participation is illustrated by **special invitees**, including Jayant Chaudhary in Skill/Employment/Livelihood and Jitendra Singh in Accommodation. Special invitee status differs from committee membership.

## 4. Groups of Ministers (GoMs)

- **GoM:** ministers brought together for an identified cross-ministry issue; investigates/co-ordinates and recommends. An **empowered GoM** may decide within explicitly delegated authority. Concerned portfolio ministers participate; task-bound groups may be disbanded after completion.
- These are different from the standing Cabinet Committees. Neither the number nor existence of particular GoMs is permanent.
- **Second ARC (2005–2009), Organisational Structure of Government report (2009):** too many GoMs, irregular meetings and unfinished work caused delays. Recommended **selective use, clear mandates, prescribed deadlines and effective coordination**; decision-making authority where appropriate. Commission chaired by **Veerappa Moily**.
- **31 May 2014:** government abolished the then-existing **9 EGoMs + 21 GoMs**, returning pending issues to ministries/departments with Cabinet Secretariat/PMO facilitation. This historical decision did **not** remove the Rules’ provision allowing later ad hoc GoMs. [PIB announcement](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?lang=2&reg=48&relid=105321).

## 5. One-minute recall

- **Cabinet = constitutional definition in 352(3); Cabinet Committees = business-rule bodies; GoMs = issue-specific coordination.**
- **Standing ≠ immutable; ad hoc ≠ standing; recommendation ≠ only function; delegation ≠ unlimited power.**
- **Eight now; six PM-headed; Accommodation—Home; Parliamentary Affairs—Defence. ACC = two members; Security = PM + four key ministers.**
- Mains: committee system improves specialisation/speed; safeguards are inter-ministry consultation, clear authority, Cabinet review and time-bound coordination.

## Reference

- [Transaction of Business Rules: Rule 6 and First Schedule](https://www.cabsec.gov.in/writereaddata/transactionofbusinessrulescomplete/completeaobrules/english/1_Upload_3983.pdf).
